i highly recommend dr. goldman. early this year (2020), he performed cataract surgery on both my eyes. the experience was pleasant and with excellent results. for 70 years my driver's license restricted me to driving only with corrective lenses. (yes, i'm 85.). i had substantial correction for astigmatism and nearsightedness. i now have 20/30 vision in one 20/25 in the other. i passed the eye exam at mvd and no longer have a restricted license. i will get a prescription for 20/20 vision in both eyes and for reading, but i may never buy glasses. so far, i see up close and my computer using $20 readers from walgreens. 

i was terrified at the prospect of eye surgery. fifteen months earlier, i canceled cataract surgery at the last minute.  dr. g patiently and with graciousness allowed me to try again. he and his staff had to work me up once again. they were very professional in doing so; they didn't give me a hard time, though i felt they had every right to do so. 

surgery took place at a beautiful new facility just east of pima road and north of via de ventura.  the staff there is different from dr. g's office staff and care for the patients of several doctors. nonetheless, i was made to feel as if they were dr. g's exclusive staff. 

i was guided to a bed separated from other beds by a curtain. a nurse prepped me by installing a port (hope that's correct because my memory of what happens next begins to grow dim due to partial retrograde amnesia - like having a colonoscopy where you're awake but later don't remember being awake). 

i didn't have to change into hospital garb; i even kept my shoes on. they had me lie on a freshly made gurney (not a hospital bed) and gave me a light blanket. i remember meeting the anesthesiologist, who was kind and comforting as i confessed my terror. my next memory is dr. g taping a cup-like device over my eye. he was all done!!  wtf?

i have absolutely no recollection of the surgery.  if asked. i will say i was out; however, dr. g insists i was conscious and talking during the procedure. just like during a colonoscopy.  it was like magic. if i was anxious during the procedure, i have no recollection of it. i assure you i was anything but brave going into it. years ago, my sister told me that when she had cataract surgery she was so far in nana land she felt no anxiety. that helped me. but what assuaged my fear the most was dr. g's competence (he'd been my doctor for several years), the attendant staff and the clean surroundings.

having survived the first surgery, i returned for the second two weeks later - this time without the anxiety of the first. 

i'm not a rookie to surgery. i've had six coronary by-passes, eight coronary stents, a pacemaker, back surgery and surgery for testicular cancer. i was more apprehensive about this procedure than any of the others. there's something about the eyes that scares the you-know-what out of me.  

fear not, however. if you choose dr. g, you'll be in excellent hands. better than a tranquilizer.

i have a number of autoimmune disorders and take a very heavy-duty immunosuppressant plus another daily, weaker med that does the same thing. so when i get sick, i get significantly sicker than your average patient. i went to the minute clinic last week with a severely swollen and sore throat, low-grade fever, evidence of infection in my sinuses, cough and inflamed lymph nodes. saw a nurse practitioner who took a strep culture and gave me lidocaine for the throat. i have no issue with her treatment, as i feel waiting for results was reasonable.

however, the next day (which is now five days after i initially got sick), i was significantly worse. at this point, my tonsils were swollen so badly, i was worried about it affecting my breathing and i called to see if she could prescribe something while we waited for the strep test. it was a different np this day and she refused to even speak with me and, as it was relayed to me, was "annoyed" i hadn't gone through "proper channels" to ask my question. 

later that day, the strep culture came back negative. the nurse still refused to speak with me, told me through her lpn that it was a virus that just needed to "run its course" and wouldn't listen when i tried to explain that my immune system isn't going to be able to fight it without some medical intervention.

the following day, now day 6, i was still worse, but now i was having chest pain and difficulty breathing. at this point, i went to urgent care and saw an actual doctor who immediately recognized i needed help. he diagnosed me with strep (and told me that a huge percentage of strep cultures give a false negative because they aren't collected properly) that was rapidly developing into pneumonia, plus a bad case of pink eye. 

it's been almost a week now that i've been on antibiotics, steroids and eye drops and i'm slowly recovering. a lot of this could have been avoided, had the provider at cvs actually listened to me and taken my illness seriously. i understand a viral infection won't respond to antibiotics, but the nurse didn't even offer a steroid. she didn't show any care or concern at all. i definitely won't be going back to any minute clinic, as i felt the level of care was very poor.

my pcp recommended dr. jane wolford, who now works with this eye center, but based on his knowledge of her back when she had her own private practice.

i was incredibly disappointed with my experiences, though i suspect they have more to do with the support staff than with dr. wolford herself.

it started when i was first called back into the exam area, where one of the technicians began one of those automatic diagnostics of my prescription. the tech asked me if i was okay with being dilated - which, i figured they needed to ask permission because i would incur an additional charge for dilation. i agreed to pay for dilation, and the tech went ahead and dilated my eyes *before seeing the doctor.*

a short while later, i was in the room, meeting with dr. wolford. one of the reasons she was recommended to me specifically was for her experience with aging eyes. i am over 40 and really having difficulty with my extreme close up vision. i was hoping to specifically address this concern with the doctor.

however - she couldn't address my close-up vision because i had been dilated. dilation makes it so that your eyes can't see close up.

lo and behold, the easiest option was to make a second appointment.

hellooooooo, insurance fraud anyone?? if they had simply waited to dilate my eyes until after seeing the doctor, i could have gotten everything done in one visit. 

okay, no big deal, so i get a second visit, right? 

wrong. at my second visit, guess what? their entire computer system for the entire center had been attacked by a virus and was inaccessible. all the notes from my previous visit weren't available. 

the doctor saw me anyway, did another exam on me, and within 2 seconds declared that i didn't need bifocals (in other words, sorry, you're stuck with your crappy close up vision because old age sucks) and and and ... 

why was i even there?!? why couldn't they have called me that morning to alert me that their system was down and if they couldn't access records, they wouldn't be able to provide me with a quality visit? or if they didn't have access to their appointment information, why not explain to me during check-in that it would be best for me to reschedule for another day? or, why not wait to dilate your patients until after the doctor checks their dang vision???

anyway, after seeing the doctor i try taking my new prescription to the in-house optical center, only to find out that they can't use my current frames, i would need to either pick new frames or go back to the original practice that sold me my frames.

and of course, i got billed for that second visit.

maybe these are all things that are circumstantial, and mostly out of the doctor's control ... but i was so annoyed by the whole thing, i'll be looking for yet another place nearby to get my eyes fixed (this place was the third in longmont that i've tried, and i have yet to get glasses that actually correct my vision).

p.s. i went just now to see the info page on dr. wolford over at the eye center's website - she has a little video there on how she can test for dry eyes. i have always thought that i have dry eyes, but i've never been tested for it. maybe if i don't actually have dry eyes, i might be a candidate for lasik? in any case, i wasn't offered any sort of testing that wolford describes on their website.

frustrating. 30 minute + call hold times without any success in reaching an actual human being; when you finally reach someone, they transfer you around or place you on hold again. frustrating to make an appointment and especially when you need to cancel or reschedule an appointment.

physicians here are ok, and depending on your specific condition(s) some are better than others. doctors here give a lot of lip service about how much clinical knowledge they have about specific conditions but understanding may be on a superficial level. doctors here tend to bulk conditions together as well as the associated treatments, sometimes grouping conditions together and making statements that "this and that condition is the same as this condition", when in fact they are nothing alike. doctor's here also look at the patient in pieces rather than a whole system and there are times when you may communicate your source of pain very explicitly, because you of course know your body the best, only to have it dismissed by the doctor as something else or originating elsewhere. after testing only later to be told that you were correct and that you were accurately describing the pain and its location. lol.

lots of pushing shots, which are incredibly painful during and post procedure-- these shots don't have any long term studies on long term effects. shots containing steroids and injected close to the structures of the spine may have the potential to cause additional tissue weakness, osteoporosis or early onset osteoarthritis at the location and/or surrounding location. this can be especially common in those with certain bone and connective tissue disorders/conditions. depending on one's drug metabolism, type of disorder or condition, etc shots may not be as effective for everyone. ime after a round of very painful shots, the side effects that appeared hours later and lasted two weeks were unmanageable. in my case the shots offered no relief relief at all and (in my opinion) turned out to be a waste of money..

other options include pt which always has potential to worsen certain conditions and cause additional damage or injury if the therapist doesn't have a clue about your condition and lumps you in with all the other folks with the same diagnosis code on their order. next option may be actual pain management using medications. of course certain medications require you to sign a guilty plea, i mean contact that can come off as incredibly limiting and sadistic-- which can make normal folks feel like they're doing something wrong by trying to seek relief from their pain with medications that actually work for them. the contract is in place to cover the practices butt mostly and to deter doctor shopping and drug seeking behavior from the folks who need legitimate pain control. the contract is no big deal as long as you follow the guidelines, don't mind peeing in a cup at every visit and being billed for the urine screening.

the contract also requires you to choose one pharmacy and to only use that specific pharmacy; you'll also spend a lot of time over the phone making calls and over explaining, with a mouth full of cotton wedges, to the dentist that just pulled all four of your wisdom teeth that you can't take that script for percocet because you signed a pain contract. then you'll need to power through the dentist's look of distain and explain to that same dentist that she/he needs to call your pain management doctor to let them know that they need to prescribe the medication for your dental extractions. while under the contract you cannot receive opioids from anywhere else, not the er, not the dentist, etc. outside prescribing doctors need to coordinate with your doctor at national spine & pain and s&p will decide if you need the prescription and they will be the one to prescribe it to you. so, lots of anxiety inducing complications and extra steps may occur with the contract if you decide to go that route.

shots and prescribing medications about sums up this practice. if you're looking for services like bracing, the office staff nor doctors offer any assistance with evaluating/choosing bracing, sizing nor ordering of braces, joint splits, etc. physicians aren't all too interested in assisting patients with these requests-- i guess you can't blame them since fluoroscopy assisted procedures involving x-rays, long probes and pricey lidocaine/steroid shots do make a whole lot more money for them than helping a patient fit and choose a joint stabilization device.

my stonington experience started with the detox. 9 days. they use ativan for alcohol detox. they tapered me too fast which resulted in an er visit and 7 days in a psychiatric hospital where i was given valium to taper more appropriately. 

i spent about 20 hours at the rehab in groton after the detox. the withdrawal from the ativan hit at 11pm, and i didn't get seen by the psychiatrist until almost 10am. i didn't sleep for 40 hours straight between the detox, the 20 hours at the rehab and getting a bed at the hospital. i spoke to 3 people in trails corner about my condition and got no help whatsoever. when i finally had sat through a 15 minute class on handwashing and walked over to the other building i talked to the clinician who finally listened to me and thought a man in severe withdrawal and suicidal thoughts might need help. i then saw the psychiatrist who called the ambulance. 

concerning the environment at the rehab dormitory:
-there are no actual clinical staff available.
-each room has about 12 bunk beds and 1 bathroom. 
-the windows are almost all frosted like a shower door so you get light, but you can't see outside. 
-there is no visitation except for court ordered dcf visits 
-you can only get stuff dropped off between 10am and 2pm m-f.
-drugs are sold and used. 
-the staff is indifferent at best.
-it took 6 days to get them to send my belongings to the hospital.
-they failed to send my medications that i had brought there.
-they assigned me to a top bunk. i am 6'3" 230lbs, late 40's with back issues. i asked to be given a bottom bunk within 20 minutes of being there and was told i needed a doctor's order to change the bed. 
-no hygienic products are provided. 
-no electronic devices are allowed, including mp3 players.
-there is no comfortable or quiet place to sit; either lay in bed or sit on plastic chairs with a tv mounted 10 feet up on the wall. 
-the gym was not open.

you know, no ones really ever thrilled about being in an er. there are classically long waits, sick people coughing all over you, and no one ever brings you that martini you ordered. i can't say that for most people a trip to the er will be a pleasurable experience, but i think if you take into account what to expect from such a visit and adjust your parameters, you can still end up with a 4-5 star experience. 

as coronavirus is running rampant in wa right now, i really wasn't inclined to visit a doctor when my clumsy self fell running and my finger turned 50 shades of purple..yah not at all sultry or enticing as an ombre of grey. i taped and generally avoided until i couldn't any longer and checked myself into the er with an xray of my translocated finger break..so apparently a purple finger is not a sign its healing normally just fyi.

the ladies at the front were positively peachy and got me checked in and even gave me the mask i requested to avoid the dreaded beer virus (cv). i really loved the new construction of the building with modern aesthetics, the checkin desk being separate from the waiting space and the door that begins your journey into the next waiting space.

i actually didn't hang out in the waiting room too long and an rn nabbed me to triage. he checked out my radiograph i came prepared with and laughed at my attempt to convince myself i was totally fine. they moved me after vitals to a nice patient room with a tv playing relaxing music and showing gorgeous scenery photography, i actually quite enjoyed that touch. the room was modern, clean, and had rather nice cabinetry. 

radiology popped in after hardly any wait to snap a few more photos of my mangled paw and then came the long wait for the physician. i  waited about 40 mins or so for her to pop in, say yah..that's a pretty complicated break.. then another 25 mins or so as she stepped out to see if there was anything she could do for me.

i was disappointed i couldn't be treated for a fracture there but i am ignorant to the extensive training in all disciplines that an er physician has so perhaps this is normal. what i did appreciate was she was able to secure me a last min visit at the end of day, on a friday no less, with a hand surgeon. she reviewed my case with him, sent the radiographs, and i was on my way to bellevue for a splint. 

im sure i won't like the bill for this adventure, but again i think adjusting expectations to fit emergency care wait, limitations, and costs is a must. i was pleased as a whole with the speed of the triage, the attempts of the physician to get me to where i needed to be, and the friendly rns and front desk personnel that made my experience as pleasant as possible. so what did we learn kids? purple fingers are bad, see a doctor.

my wife had a very debilitating illness which came on somewhat suddenly just before christmas.  she is usually in very good health, but whatever she had knocked her flat.  she had visited dr. fang for a physical in the past, but never had the need to see her for anything else.    we got in to see her very quickly for an examination.
her bedside manner is exceptional.  she is patient, inquisitive and, most importantly, very thorough as she questions you.  we never felt rushed or ignored and she allowed my wife to explain her symptoms completely.  her initial diagnosis had a few scary possibilities, so she began ordering tests.  she was apologetic when explaining that she was going on vacation until after the new year and that the ucla system (like every other business during the holidays) would be running at reduced capacity.
understandably, at this point, we were even more concerned.  when facing systemic delays during a health scare, you're left with your mind racing to various awful outcomes and to be denied expediency at such a time is devastating.  and, of course, dr. internet is telling you bye-bye; you're toast.
dr, fang sensed our trepidation and with the help of pedro and christina in her office, scheduled all the tests, imaging and specialist visit in such short order that we were completely reassured.  in addition, she personally called us 3 times to discuss each set of test results and to continue her path to diagnosis while she was on vacation.
i can't stress just how reassuring knowing that your doctor was following up personally as opposed to justifiably handing your case off to a covering physician and letting us simmer until business resumed two weeks later.
i was somewhat reticent to post this review fearing that others would seek her out and increase her popularity to where we couldn't get in as soon as we wanted.  but when your health is on the line, you truly want someone like dr. fang and a system like ucla to have your back.

my wife and i adopted a cat. ther cat was the single most loving and snuggly cat in the history of cats. last year, the cat developed a number of health problems that required medication.  he needed 3 compounded medications. our vet recommended these folks. at first everything was fine. the vet would call me to authorize the charge on my bank card for each medication. and it was delivered on time.

i consulted with dr spoonamore in december 2019. i have ongoing siatica pain in my left leg which comes from spinal problems. i have protruding discs in the lumbar spine.  that can cause a great deal of pain. i have been treating this condition with epidural injections which do mask the pain temporarily. but i have to have an injection every 3 to 4 months to stay out of pain. i was looking for a more permanent solution. i was hoping i would be a candidate for non invasive surgery.

dr spoonamore sat with me for about 45 minutes, possibly longer,  with the cd of my mri results in front of us on his computer screen. he gave me a nuanced consultation about the kind of surgery i would need to remove the bulging discs and he advised against surgery.  unfortunately, dr spoonamore does not think that i am not a candidate for non invasive procedures because the location of the discs are too close to the spine.  so, according to him, i would need to have a fusion. that would mean they would have to go through bone and muscle to remove the discs.  dr spoonamore explained that would be a long and painful recovery. and, that i may not even be out of pain when recovery was complete, because he would not be able to remove all of the protruding discs in one operation. he said i may need a second surgery to remove the remaining discs.  

dr spoonamore recommended that i continue with quarterly injections if that is helping to mask the pain.  and, that i start up with physical therapy.  to give me hope, he said that stem cell therapy may be a viable option in the future.

update: i'm no stranger to surgeries and medical procedures, but so many of them have gone poorly for me, either by being painful or ineffective or mistakes being made. this was my first elective medical procedure and the only one that went smoothly and painlessly. the most painful part of this procedure was peeling the tape off my face to lift the eye shields up to put eye drops in. 

getting the valium was a big help to my anxiety and took away my restless/fidgety nature so i could lay still during the procedure. this team seemed liked a well oiled machine; they communicated concisely and calmly and it was incredibly comforting to know what was going on and how long it would take for each step. when i heard "18 seconds," i felt extremely relieved, not just because that step was extremely short, but also because i knew what to expect. the team had an awesome sense of humor and had me laughing for half the procedure. there was pressure, there was discomfort, but there wasn't any pain and i don't think the entire procedure took 5 minutes. i kept my eyes closed for a few hours after, but when i woke up and lifted the eye shields, i could see, perfectly, and that's amazing. 

my friend was able to sit in a waiting room and watch/record the procedure on a tv, which was so cool. i've watched the video like 5 times already and i just can't believe the coordination and care they're able to achieve.

i have 20/20 vision the day after the procedure, with no pain or dryness. to prepare for the surgery i took fish oil, lutein, and zeaxanthin, used preservative free eye drops generously as well as msm eyedrops daily and used a steam mask daily. i've been giving my eyes a full 30 seconds closed at the beginning of every hour to be sure i don't experience the dryness or discomfort that i've read some others do. i'm not sure if all the prepping i did contributed to how smoothly it went, but i know it went a long way toward making my eyes feel better regardless.

as a community member, i don't feel los robles provided even minimally acceptable service. i looked on their website for a place to lodge complaints but there isn't one. interesting. additionally, there are more "1" ratings of this hospital on this site than "5" ratings. i'm not surprised by that.  i'm sure there will be an insipid follow up comment from jasmin o. saying "thank you for your comment, sorry we didn't meet your expectations" or something noncommittal like that. the fact that the hospital offers the same canned response to every poor review indicates to me that there is a lack of true caring.

everyone has bad days at work, i get that. but in certain industries, that can be dangerous. you don't want ticked off air traffic controllers, lackadaisical nuclear energy plant operators, or medical staff who lack compassion and don't really want to help patients. i expected more out of the er. we won't return; we'll go to an urgent care spot if needed in the future. which is too bad since los robles loses a future chance to over bill our very generous insurance company.

i'd like to preface this by stating that i've never been very fond of doctors, am very skeptical of big pharma, and have always tried holistic/ alternative methods first whenever struck with ailments.

once again, you all know it has to be bad for me to haul myself to urgent care. in this case, it was 12 days of cold and flu symptoms, running the gamut from chest-rattling cough, runny nose with snot in a variety of different colors (sorry!), fever and what i'd call laryngitis. 

i had picked up something nasty, either on a flight from dublin to london, a flight from london to vegas, or from one of the thousands of people who insisted on shaking hands during ces. whatever the cause, i was suffering, and it was lingering. i figured i should get looked at, in case it was something crazy (and this was a few weeks before the news of the coronavirus hit...)

the waiting room was pretty packed when i got there, with a handful of people wearing surgical masks. a sign at check-in asked those exhibiting cold or flu symptoms to don a mask, so i followed suit.

check-in was fast and painless, once i got past the forms. after turning in my completed documents, i sat in one of the chairs, trying not to cough too loudly or blow my nose too often, waiting for my name to get called.

it actually didn't take very long, given the number of people in line ahead of me. the intake nurse brought me back for vitals, and to ask all the necessary questions. she then sat me down in a room and told me the doctor would be right with me.

want to hear something crazy? i spent more time typing that paragraph above than the doctor spent on me. he listened to the rattle in my chest, asked me a couple of questions, then diagnosed bronchitis and a sinus infection. he told me to meet him at the lobby, and we were done.

i had to ask the nurse to ask the doctor if i was contagious. to his credit, he came back out to the front to answer my question (he called me "close contact contagious", meaning i shouldn't share drinks with or kiss people, but said i'd be fine in normal situations.)

it was an okay experience, but here i am, 24 days after my visit, still working to shake the cough. my husband says i need to get to my regular doctor. he's probably right. maybe i'll make that appointment soon.

the healthcare providers here are nice enough but management-wise there is room for improvement. similar to another review here, after my physical last year i received notice that my tests -- which i hadn't completed -- came back normal. in addition, while the front/back office is computerized, the patient charts are not. some of the physician's assistants spend more time than others making sure they review what other pas/doctors have documented in the chart. 

there's truth to the saying "nobody knows your body like you do". all these years, even though i have asthma, i have kept myself out of the hospital. although i have been a patient at this practice nearly a year, it has taken me some time to adapt to the presence of so many physician's assistants, which at times has made it feel like i'm reinventing the wheel (especially when they don't spend enough time reviewing the chart before the visit begins). 

in general, i do wish there was more effort to accommodate patients with chronic conditions and/or disabilities who simply want to manage them proactively. as an example, i attempted after the 7.2 earthquake in july last year to put together an emergency kit -- which for where i live is supposed to consist of a month's worth of food, water, supplies and medications -- but i had trouble stocking it with my medications because there's no allowance for this. worse, my spouse and i have hit some major car trouble over the past year and since we live in a rural area without bus service (or even semi-affordable uber) there have been times i do not have transportation. the other problem is that this office has a strict policy of seeing the patient for medication refills vs. treatment. a typical situation is that my refill appointment is already scheduled so when i come down sick i have to choose between medication and treatment.

i have been told that my only option in such situations is a secondary office visit -- even if i've been in recently and/or don't have access to transportation. this is frustrating because prior to moving to this area my former primary care physician of over 20 years worked with me, not against me, in extenuating circumstances. i want to continue my track record of managing my asthma well enough, even through flu season, to remain out of the hospital. sadly, i feel that effort is not accommodated -- chiefly because this office does not allow for remote (phone/video) consultation. (if you're lucky, a nurse will call you back. if you're not, it's possible to leave multiple messages and/or for your calls to go straight to voicemail even during normal business hours.)

it is one thing to expect patients to show up regularly for care -- which is reasonable -- another to mandate that all patients, regardless of health risks, even in flu season, make what amounts to revolving-door use of the (sick) patient waiting room. given recent news of a public health emergency, my concern is that allowing patient calls to reach a voicemail system, where their best efforts to leave a message may go unreturned, will open up this practice to seeing patients who should have been evaluated, at least on a preliminary basis, by phone. instead, it is my impression that the office doesn't really track why the patient has scheduled an appointment. cdc guidelines in dealing with the emerging coronavirus threat, as an example, recommends that medical providers ask patients to "call ahead" to prepare for their arrival (to limit exposure to staff and other patients). if patient calls are unreturned, the staff doesn't note why the patient has made an appointment and there is no phone consultation option, staff may eventually be forced by the cdc to take time off work to self-quarantine thanks to reflexively advising patients to simply show up for an office visit regardless of the reason for their visit.

while i sympathize that doctor's offices are already subjected to more calls than they care to take, that doesn't mean patients who have successfully managed chronic health conditions for many years should be held to a rigid policy aimed at compelling every patient, regardless of health status or extenuating circumstance, to show up as per usual -- even in the midst of a county/state emergency declaration. during a recent period without my car -- spouse's car was at the dealer for more than a month for an airbag recall and an unrelated repair -- i was more than willing to schedule a follow up visit but had no way to get there. my requests for a callback kept going to voicemail until i got high desert medical group to connect me to the front office. when i explained my circumstances, i expected to be connected to a nurse. instead i was told that there was nothing that would be done unless i scheduled a second in-person visit. my pleas for a reasonable accommodation were flatly denied. this left me feeling patronized and confused. nobody ought to feel like that when seeking health "care".

doc_text:
dr robert krage, dc

interview
i fell for the full-page ad in the desert sun last january 2019. although i thought dcs should stick to spinal care, but here was a dc who seemed able to treat foot problems.  i have had morton's neuromas for 8 years, treated with alcohol injections which reduced them somewhat, but they still bothered me. dr. krage's initial consultation is like a pep rally to motivate one to "qualify" for his treatment plan based on willingness to follow through with the plan and reap the huge benefits - much like a timeshare presentation. he also videos your walking on a treadmill and tells you that you are doing it wrong and that is why you have 'hammer toes', which sounded dubious to me. still, i wanted to believe that he could help my discomfort so i continued. one of the tests he performed was to dig his thumb into the bottom of my heel until i yelled in pain. that, he said, was "plantar fasciitis".  really?? that was the only time i ever had pain in my heel!! the 2nd consultation requires the spouse or significant other to attend, presumably to acknowledge joint willingness to pay the high cash fee up front without dissent.   the contract he presents starts at over $15,000 but - of course - he mentions "discounts" (for no apparent reason) which brings it down to $7,000.  when $15,000 would be an "absolutely not!" answer, agreeing to $7,000 is not quite so bitter to swallow - with a big dose of hope!

treatments:
all treatments, whether laser for feet or backs, or stretching for those with spinal problems - are done by the hardworking, organized and caring 2 office attendants at a satellite office on fred waring in palm desert. (his main office is in corona.) for me these included lasers directed to the soles of my feet and strong percussion treatments before or after, 3 times per week for 32 sessions.  dr krage did just a few foot percussion treatments and took molds for the expensive, high quality orthotics that were made to order. otherwise i rarely saw him other than to say 'hello'.
when the 1st set of orthotics arrived i tried to use them in my shoes for the 2 hour periods, but could not sustain the daily schedule due to the discomfort. i never got to the 4 hour or 6 hour daily sessions, and never picked up my 2nd custom set of orthotics -- which were supposed to be even more severe in pushing up my metatarsal arches.

results:
i can't attest to how laser treatments may or may not have helped the other patients in this office, most of whom received the treatments on their lumbar backs, but for my morton's neuromas, i found no benefit whatsoever. i regret ever being so optimistic that dr krage's  full-page splashy ad convinced me that an amazing new treatment would do more for the painful lumps in the balls of my feet than my podiatrist could do.   if i had researched yelp.com sooner, and searched for his san diego connection to a similar treatment claim in another krage office in previous years. i would have run the other way.
even recently in the coachella valley, dr krage was fined for "false advertising" in 2014.  at $7000 per patient, a $300 fine is easy to pay!  https://search.dca.ca.gov/details/8500/dc/24734/7cfefa3ed5e1338723892475e4bcfe7d 
dr krage does not take any insurance as payments -- most likely, because his treatments are not approved by any medical or government authority. i completely wasted $7000, plus a lot of time.
 
also, robert krage dc may be related to john krage dc of san diego since robert is linked to a san diego chiropractic office years ago on the internet. 
the following is noteworthy from the california board of chiropractors webpage of professional violations.
krage, john-san diego dc 14672 12/30/2013     gross negligence; repeated negligence acts; false advertising; excessive treatment; dishonesty; use of laser for purposes other than those approved by the us food and drug administration (fda)  https://www.chiro.ca.gov/about_us/summer_2014.pdf

and decades ago there was another john krage in san diego with the same ads and the same "happy feet" logo. that dc is retired or deceased but is probably the father with 2 sons who followed his  business model.

rushed my mother to williamson medical at 1 am this morning hoping to get relief from the writhing pain she was experiencing related to bladder cancer. despite having only one other patient, the er team was cold, harsh, thoughtless and entirely lacking in empathy. they were also mistaken in key parts of their diagnosis and their treatment. 

based on my experience today, i would never send a relative or a friend to williamson medical under any circumstance imaginable. 

why do these "healthcare professionals" feel they are serving their patients if they allow interminable delays (we were left for 2 hours without getting pain medication of any kind - the very reason we went in the first place) and brutish bedside manners (being moved from bed to gurney like a sack of potatoes, my mother getting screamed at during insertion of a catheter, blaming the patient for difficulty finding a vein {it took 3 tries and 3 pokes} in which to insert an iv, etc.).  10-minutes into the nurse screaming catheter insertion i heard the head nurse, amy, finally ask my mother what her name was. think about that. 

i found medical trash strewn all over the room we were in. this is 3rd world treatment and 3rd world quality care. 

i have great reverence for those who commit their lives to the serving and healing of strangers. i revere and feel hfriends who are er doctors, social workers, cancer scientists. these people serve mankind and they have empathy somehow baked into their dna. the er team at williamson medical should seriously consider why they chose to serve the public. i wouldn't hire any of the nurses or the doctor we dealt with to deliver my mail - they'd find a way to screw it up. they might, however, be just right to pick up our trash curbside.

to be fair, i should note we had generally positive experiences from the er check-in staff. also had acceptable treatment and care after getting my mother checked into the main hospital. but by the time we were upstairs, we had lost faith in the entire place, so we were watching/prodding them closely to be sure they attended properly to our mom. no one should need to do that. 

later in the day i spoke to an emt who said he wouldn't allow his friends or family to get taken to williamson medical er, that they have an awful reputation as a dumping ground for patients who have no advocacy and no close family oversight. his quote was "tell them to take you farther north to vandy, st. thomas etc. ". he also said, "even if you arrive at williamson medical without an infection, you'll surely leave with one". yikes.  wish i'd known. that's why i've labored over this review. beware. 

and my heart goes out to anyone reading this who has a loved one suffering like my mother has. god bless.

i came here with a long history of snoring (according to my family), sleepiness during the day, tired, weight gain, and feeling depressed.  my sleep study revealed severe sleep apnea, and i knew myself well enough to know that i would/could not tolerate a cpap mask.  in fact, the reason i came here was because they offered options to cpap.

i was fitted with a dental appliance that made a huge difference in not only how i sleep, but also in how i feel. dr. joe explained what sleep apnea is and how it affects all parts/systems of the body - the brain, the stress hormones, the weight gain, mental fogginess/forgetfulness.  before long, i started "feeling like my old self", better than i had in at least a decade!  i began to have more energy because my body was able to get restorative sleep.  the clouds lifted, my mental clarity improved, and i began losing weight.  with my energy level improved,  i actually felt like exercising again!   my stress hormones went down because i wasn't struggling so hard to breathe in my sleep.  because of the severity of my sleep apnea, i also got a supplemental nasal device called bongo which has been a great complement to my oral device.  my followup sleep study was greatly improved!  i still snore sometimes, but my family says the difference is night and day from how it was before i got treatment.  the best part is no confining mask, no tubes, and no machine.

every single interaction i have had with every single person at sleep medicine group has been professional and courteous.  i cannot think of one negative.  they handled all the insurance for me and there have been no surprises.  

if you snore or are chronically tired, i strongly encourage you to get checked out here.  treating sleep apnea has never been easier.  you do not need a referral - you can refer yourself.  sleep medicine group is state of the art and cutting edge and the pnw is very fortunate to have such a great resource here!

i was brought back to the testing area as routine.  since it's drug testing, there are particular about a lot of things (emptying pockets, etc) to help ensure the validity of the tests.  i was told to hang my jacket and place wallet/keys/phone into a lock box.   then i was given instructions on how to fill the cup and they marked it with a red line.   you are not allowed to use the sink while in the bathroom (this is important below). 

i was able to get mostly to the red line and toward the end of the urine stream i realized i didn't quite have enough urine.  as such, i gave a squeeze and got some out of the cup onto my hands (ugh, i can't believe i just pissed on myself).   so i get some paper towel to open the door handle and take the sample out.   i let the guy know and move to wash my hands at another sink, he says i'm not allowed to do that until i go through a procedure check (i have to watch him pour the urine and seal the sample).  this is pretty standard stuff, so no big deal.   

then he asks me to sign paperwork.  i started to walk to another sink to wash my hands which had a small amount of urine on them and he says i need to stop otherwise "i've refused the test and it's now invalid".  i clarify with him that i will be touching the pen with urine on my hands, he said not to worry (presumably since they will wipe the pen).   after going through several more steps, i am able to wash my hands.   i do so, and am instructed to now collect my things.  

now this is the part that gets unusual/confusing to me.  i collect my belongings and let him know that there's still urine on the pen that he had me use.   urine is usually sterile (unless you have a uti), but still ... i recommended that he wipe it down.  he actually said "it's ok, we've got gloves and we're safe".    i said it's not for your safety, it's for the next person who's now touching the pen with piss on it.   he had no comment but went to get the next person for testing.   he also didn't change his gloves between people.   it's for this reason i think they deserve a low rating. 

i am surprised that a testing facility has such sloppy sanitary procedures.  even after pointing out the deficiency, the person seemed ambivalent to the issue.  seems like this could be a good opportunity to help train and educate the staff on better and more meticulous specimen handling procedures.   anyhow, i thought i would pass this on in the hopes that anyone using this facility understands that they do not as a matter of routine follow minimum standards for handling.  this is certainly more acutely important given the recent infection and pandemic concerns, etc.  

good luck peeps and i hope the review helps!

2019 was a very tough year for me indeed, being told you need a multi-level fusion was my worst nightmare. * weeks ago, on november 20, 2019 dr. serge obukhoff changed my life forever, this is my story. 11 years ago, i was involved in a car accident that damaged disc c4 and c5. a year after the accident it was determined that the brachial plexus nerves had been compromised and i began to lose function in my right arm. a kaiser surgeon then recommended i undergo a laminectomy to relive pressure on the brachial plexus to regain function of my arm. surgery was simply not an option for me as i had several friends and former athletes that had undergone various spine surgeries and the results were terrible. i found a great chiropractor and started yoga and other homeopathic remedies.

my symptoms were masked for the next 10 years and i enjoyed regular fitness and sporting activities. i played in several basketball and volleyball leagues as well maintained my regular gym regiment. i felt good for the most part but still dealt with numbness in my right arm. in 2019 that same numbness became worse and i also started to feel numbness in my left hand. headaches and dizziness also became regular symptoms as clearly something was not going well for me neurologically. i visited a neurosurgeon local to me and another mri was performed. the results of this scan were terrible as now the damaged disc included c4, c5, c6 and c7. the herniation of these disc had now begun to bruise my spinal cord and images on the mri showed a potential for significant paralysis if any additional damage occurred. 

this doctor said my only option was a multi-level (3 level) fusion and that he also wanted to perform a laminectomy to relieve pressure on my spinal cord. the surgery needed to be performed immediately and he wanted me in the hospital asap. after another consultation it seemed a fusion was my only option and my prognosis seemed bleak. as an athlete a 3-level fusion is game changer and my activities post-surgery would certainly be limited. thank god that one night late i spent time on the internet doing research on artificial disc for spine injuries. i found incredible videos on the mobi-c device by zimmer biomet. this device was successfully being used for multi-level spine injuries as an effective treatment option. through more research i was able to locate dr. serge obukhoff and my life has been completely transformed. he spent so much time with me in his beverly hills office going over my injury and explaining exactly what my options were. with great care we put together a plan to attack my injury and still maintain mobility in my neck to continue my active lifestyle. 

the surgery lasted 4 hours and the moment i woke up for the first time in 10 years i could feel my right arm. all the numbness was gone, and i can say i got extremely emotional being able to feel my son hold my right hand in the recovery room. the last 8 weeks i have made incredible strides and i can proudly say i am pain free for the first time in years! i am getting stronger every day and should be cleared to full activity in the next few weeks. let me say again i am pain free and have full feeling in my right and left arm. i have been able to walk at least 4 miles every day for the last 3 weeks and i am dying to start running and lifting soon. dr. serge obukhoff is an incredibly gifted surgeon who gave me my life back and for that i am forever grateful. i would highly recommend him for any procedure but especially recommend him for complex multi-level procedures. there is simply no one better!

i finish my ct scan of my lungs and the tech comes out and says to me "we've just gotten off the phone with your doctor and he wants you to go immediately to mountain view hospital er"; you've got a pulmonary embolism in your lower left lobe.

so, i arrive at mv er and the team immediately takes me in, runs an ekg, takes blood, and performs an xray of my lungs; i was never alone.  because all er's are flooded with patients it doesn't surprise me to find myself rolled to an "easy chair" in the hallway of the er where i have to wait for a room to open up in the hospital.  3 hours later.... after being checked on frequently, they roll me into 5014 --- single room, huge, even has a couch that folds down to a twin so that my wife, if she had wanted to, could have spent the night!  surperb staff !  friendly, concerned, attentive, and helpful.  i spent the next few nights in 5014, getting my iv heparin, frequent vital checks, blood testing to check the heparin balances.  food, did i mention that they have great food delivery?  you order from a pretty wide menu (appropriate food for why you are there, of course) but you order, they deliver within 45 minutes of your order (usually sooner).  wow.

i was there for my birthday... my day nurse made up a birthday card for me.  everyone was super sweet and caring.  my wife and i were blown away.  of course, if it takes 3 hours to get in.... yup, on discharge day i told me wife we would not leave until 3pm.... okay, we got out by 2:55pm.  overall, wonderful experience during march when the hospital is being slammed with all the usual... plus.... flu... plus corona virus worriers coming in for checkups who are "healthy"...

thanks mountain view !
martin swartout

ps
  for those who have bad experiences with the er; consider that the er must triage all cases.... based upon life threatening need.  i remember 1965, my mother was so upset (livid) that i was still laying in a gurney in the er hallway back in california after a car drove through me on my bike.... six hours later... but then, on that friday night holy cross was having to deal with huge numbers of life threatening cases due to a large gang fight where knives, chains, clubs, and the like had caused a lot of mayhem.  we all feel that our's is the most important misery, that's natural, and it is important for each of us to have an advocate insuring that we aren't ignored or forgotten... but, bottom line, the er must triage.   blessings to you all, forgive me my brief lecture.

i've been a patient of this office for around 3 years. the initial appointment was with dr. gowda who concluded i should have a sleep study based on our preliminary review of symptoms. the sleep study was comprehensive, convenient and professional. the results were undeniable. i needed a cpap machine.

all equipment, the study, and all subsequent replacement supplies have been 100% covered by medicare (with supplemental insurance). all follow-up appointments have been with the doctor's nurse practitioner, monique mulvany, and have been completely satisfactory. she carefully reviews ongoing progress and is ready to modify equipment orders at my request when improved masks become available. i've changed face mask several times to improve my comfort, and this office has made the process remarkably easy. 

it's useful to understand that after the initial study, the equipment prescription for medicare patients (and probably other insurance providers) needs to be handed off to an approved equipment supplier. that supplier, in turn, needs to receive all the appropriate forms from the medicare (or other insurer) system. the time lag is weeks. it can be frustrating. once the approvals are completed, a visit is scheduled with the supplier (xmed) which can add more time. welcome to the world of insurance and "medicare approved" suppliers. none of this takes away from what i believe was a very positive, professional experience with a very busy sleep disorder practice. i'm sleeping perfectly and the follow-up experience has been great. even that equipment supplier has proven to be reliable and thoroughly helpful, even if the initial experience was maddening.

in this time of the pandemic covid-19, it is important to acknowledge the good work and the good people we encounter.  yesterday was friday, march 19, 2020, after the official declaration of the pandemic a day or so ago, i felt it necessary to stock up on some provisions just in case.  i had the fortune of having this particular friday off.  

when i arrived at this vons location (store #2107), the parking lot was abuzz with the hums of cars and people filing into vons like many trails of ants returning to the colony.  i grabbed a shopping cart from the parking lot, expecting there would be none available just outside the sliding door.  

as i stepped through the door, the organized chaos hit me like jam onto peanut butter onto a slice of warm toast.  lots of buzzing activities with carts pushed in all directions by like minded people as myself.  i was pleased that despite the urgency in the air, shoppers and staff at this vons were pleasant to each other, but quiet. it felt like shopping for an upcoming fun holiday, but today, there was a serious undertone that permeated throughout the store.  

i pushed my cart from aisles to aisles, window shopping and wondering what i should stock up on.  i hit the main sections of frozen food, can foods, waters, can soup, cookies and snacks, but not the paper towels or toilet papers, those we already tackled at the big boy costco store last week.  

at all aisles i visited, i noticed that there was tremendous mark down in prices, offering abundance of savings. i was both surprise and happy to save on my needed supplies. 

in this time of potential crisis, vons could have easily taken advantage of their patrons like other businesses i have seen.  people are on heightened alerts for themselves and their families.  the vendors and businesses that take advantage of the pandemonium should be ashamed, and i will document those businesses for myself, and never to return in fair times.  

i stocked up on essentials such as; frozen prep meals from hungry man, marie calendars, stouffer french breads, birds eye frozen stir fry vegetables, pastas, corns, peas, can soup, water, and grapes.  this has got to go down as one of the largest single day purchase at a grocery store for me.  and at check out, my billed came out to $110.51, with a saving of $48.02. that's 30% savings.

within the coming weeks, the media will inevitably deliver alarming warning news.  it is important to be prepared, but not to hoard so that others may also get their needed foods and supplies.  our family has 10 days worth of food should san diego encounters covid-19 conditions similar to washington state and new york.  

in sharing my story, again i wanted to complement vons store #2107 and the staff for being good community members.  it is super busy at the store and the staffs are working hard to stock shelves and to get customers checked out as efficiently as possible. 

i just want to say to all members of my community, please be safe.  wash our hands thoroughly with hand soap and apply hand moisturizer (no need to pay a king's ransom for purell hand-sanitizer) , avoid touching our faces, exercise to stay healthy, get plenty of sleep, keep an eye on the children and elders in the community, be respectful to others, be calm, and do not over stress.  

we are a great community and we will weather this storm together.  god bless you and your family.  

thank you vons store #2107.

~kevin b.

my experience with dr. ransom was excellent. i've waited to post this review for over a year (my procedure was performed in november, 2018). often times final results can take up to a year and i wanted my review to be complete.

today, i asked someone at the nurse's station (i won't name names... i believe the problem is management, not entirely the fault of the individuals i'm complaining about) why it is that they don't wear masks when they enter a patient's room. she said that they're "not allowed to wear masks unless they're entering the room of someone who's in isolation, such as with tuberculosis."  not allowed?  that threw me off. i can see if maybe they let it be the nurse's option, but not allowed?  i asked to speak with the nursing supervisor on duty, and minutes later, the woman at the desk said that she called and spoke with her, but that the supervisor agreed with her that "they're not allowed" because of the low risk to them, or something like that. 

with my father's lung disease, if he were to contract the flu or a coronavirus like the now-famous covid-19, he'd be gone in days. he's a sitting duck in that place.  what's incredible to me is that my daughter wasn't allowed to visit her grandfather, because of their fairly new policy that no one under 16 y/o is allowed upstairs to the living quarters. she was confined to the parlor.  you know what?  that's a good idea. it's a shame, but schools are a mess of germs. we don't need to bombard the seniors at this place with that stuff.  but then why are we treating nurses so differently when they, too, are bombarded with germs?  are we really so naive as to believe that they have a "stronger resistance" to a new strain of coronavirus? as if nurses don't experience ups and downs with regards to their own immune systems... it's terribly insulting, or at best, it tells me that they misunderstand how a virus is spread, and the purpose of a mask with regards to spreading a virus.

my sweetheart needed an x-ray because she was feeling  icky with some onset fatigue and shortness of breath. we popped into our local urgent care for a look see. this was her first medical encounter of any kind since moving here and fortunately this facility is just down the road from us, takes our insurances and is open 24/7.

before i get into the specifics a little background is needed. i was a navy corpsman and worked in a navy er (emergency room) plus several dispensaries before working in a civilian trauma center for several years and also a paramedic driving ambulance on occasion. my sweetheart spent her college pre-med years in a catholic nursing home then 4 years in navy hospitals and 40* years in civilian hospitals (20+ at st jude) and she is a nd (doctor of naturopathic medicine) sooooo we know a little bit about urgent care and what to expect. with that said here's what happened .......   

first impressions were good with plenty of parking, large clean waiting room with masks and hand sanitizers everywhere and there's  wheelchairs available for the non-ambulatory, check. 

the receptionist ( not sure if she is the triage nurse ) is pleasant and immediately put a monitor on my honey's finger to get her o2 saturation, good. hands me some forms and they continue to take her story and assess the situation, competent triage, check.  you are informed that although this is called urgent care, they only bill your visit as an office visit. why is that important to you as a patient? they don't get into the weeds on the insurance implications but i can tell you from my years of experience that depending on your insurance carrier there could be some unexpected charges singling out individual lab test, x-rays or the physician, etc. that can also easily happen in an er today where you could be seen by several doctors (orthopedic, neurologists, radiologist, etc. and one or more might be out of network or all may be covered. it's kind of a crap shoot these days but for us we are well covered in this scenario but it's your choice, as always, whether you want to drive 20 minutes to an er and take your chances or give this place a shot.

moving on, our wait was less than 10 minutes and we went in to a small but comfortable exam room where the check-in nurse took vitals and after a few minutes the nurse practitioner arrives and takes a detailed history and orders an x-ray. without getting into personal stuff we only waited about another 20 minutes for the np comes back and tells us that the lungs and x-ray looked okay but the radiologist was backed up and that they'd call us with the official reading. she called in an antibiotic that we could opt to pick up if things got worse and we were on our way. overall it was a much more pleasant and timely experience that many er's and we feel confident with the results.    

bottom line: i am happy to report that everyone we encountered were professional and friendly and treated her with compassion and most importantly with respect. the result was exactly what we expected and we have confidence in our local urgent care facility. recommended!

logging all your food as accurately as possible is key, and mv nutrition has their own app that makes this easy.  just having the awareness of what you are actually eating makes a huge difference.

assistant device so you don't blink. your eyes are numb so you don't feel anything other than pressure and that's only while they put the device on you. the laser was on each eye maybe for 10/15 seconds they didn't spend more than 2 minutes on each eye from preparation to actual laser usage. and i was pretty blind. i used to be a -5.25 prescription and by the time i got out of the surgery room i was already seeing better than i used to with no glasses/contacts. my brother picked me up (because due to sensitivity you can't drive yourself) they advise you to go home and sleep and that's could say that i was already seeing near perfect ! the following day i felt comfortable enough to drive myself to the follow up check up where everything came out perfect. i wasn't at 20/20 yet wasn't i received an email today from this company selling covid-19 antibody testing for $350 a pop. are you serious? 

a business that i planned on checking out for a few of the things they offer, i would no longer even entertain giving my business because they are clearly not a reputable business and only care about one thing. money. 

while many other doctors in the county are providing free antibody testing to individuals, or at most charging the cost of the test only (which is nowhere near $350), these people have the nerve to try and take advantage of their community during a pandemic and seriously price gouge on a test that does nothing more than tell you if your body has the antibodies. 

even their email advertising their $350 test says "this test has been reviewed by the fda. 
negative results do not rule out sars-cov-2 infection, particularly in those who have been in contact with the virus. follow-up testing with a molecular diagnostic should be considered to rule out infection in these individuals. results from antibody testing should not be used as the sole basis to diagnose or exclude sars-cov-2 infection or to inform infection status. positive results may be due to past or present infection with non-sars-cov-2 coronavirus strains, such as coronavirus hku1, nl63, oc43, or 229e."

aka they're just trying to milk you for money by using a test that does little more than say whether you have antibodies or not and nothing else. 

really interesting they decided to start offering this a few days after the federal government announced it was mandating insurance companies to offer free antibody testing, so clearly these people are trying to make some fast cash before that gets rolled out. 

i will never support a business that tries to take advantage of the community during a crisis, let alone a pandemic, and i suggest you don't either.

in october of 2019 my best friend was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. she and her husband spent several days researching the best possible hospital. after research, and talking to medical professionals they selected the mayo clinic in rochester mn. we live in oregon so this meant a lot of travel, but they wanted the best team. their first visit with the oncologist and surgeon went very well. they returned home for her to begin a very aggressive regime of chemo. covid 19 hit so she had to have an extra round of chemo to get her follow up appointment scheduled. they risked covid exposure to fly back to rochester for their appointments. she was to get a scan on one day, and the next day see the oncologist and surgeon. the next day, upon meeting with the oncologist, she was informed her appointment with the surgeon had been cancelled. she had had no notification of this change. the reason they gave was because of covid 19. the hospital did not know what the availability of respirators would be if she could have surgery following radiation. i guess surgery for pancreatic cancer is elective surgery. you elect surgery or you die. she had several questions that the oncologist couldn't answer but said the surgeon would call her and let her know what the plan would be moving forward. she told the oncologist she would return to her room and wait for his call. he did not call, so she called his office the next day and was told he was given the message and would call her. to this day the surgeon has never reached out. my friend and her husband returned from the trip devastated. she now had no team, and no plan. fortunately ohsu and our local cancer center stepped up and took over. she has completed aggressive radiation and now waits to see if she will be able to have life saving surgery. 
my huge problem in all of this is the total lack of communication and follow through by a medical institution that is reportedly so good. how any doctor can lack so much empathy is beyond me. i feel these actions are, if not malpractice, unethical. shame all everyone at mayo involved in this, from the nurse who never notified her about the cancellation, before making the long dangerous trip, to the oncologist, who was unable answer any of her questions, and finally to the unfeeling surgeon who totally dropped the ball.

short version: phenomenal clinic. i gave birth 8 weeks ago, right when covid-19 was squeezing ny by the throat. it was a natural birth, my baby is healthy, and my body is basically back to normal - all things made possible by the expert care and support of dr brennan and his partner jais. the cliff notes on this clinic are that it is exceptional - immaculate, outstanding patient care, quirky and kind bedside manners all round, and connected to the best hospital in nyc. i cannot recommend the practice highly enough. long version: i was recommended to dr brennan by my boss (an experienced attorney who doesn't suffer fools), after i lamented the prevalence of arrogant, impersonal doctors. "you will love the brennans," my boss said. "they are eccentric, experienced, won't push an agenda, they'll give you all the time in the world, and will make you feel like family." she was right on all counts. the brennans invest seriously in their patients. throughout my pregnancy, they discussed each decision point in depth, teasing out the best path forward. perhaps because i'm a lawyer, i saw the fact that they would discuss pros and cons in front of me as a sign of true professionalism - they weren't arrogant enough to think there was one right path, and they weren't afraid to test one another's views to make sure we got it right. no question was stupid, and even if my appointment was initially 15 minutes long, they would keep answering my questions for an hour if needed. dr brennan is permanently on call for his patients, and i contacted him regularly with concerns that usually amounted to nothing but which he treated with the utmost seriousness. yes, the flipside of this kind of personal care is that appointments sometimes start late, but i would rather wait for an appointment and have this level of attention than efficiently get bad service. (and to be fair, people like me regularly rock up 45 minutes late and throw their whole schedule out of whack...).

another important plus is that dr brennan is the only doctor. in so many practices you never see the same doctor more than twice, so when you are sick they don't have a point of comparison. (nothing like being told you're fine when you feel like death). this meant that when i showed up at dr brennan's office late at night in serious pain from my contractions, he could trust right away that i wasn't playing around and needed pain relief stat. he could also read me like a book during labour - eg he suggested i use a mirror because i'm goal-orientated (and yes, it was a huge motivator!), and he knew when he could push me to the next level during delivery and when i truly needed a break from the pain. i'll always be grateful to dr brennan for staying so in tune with me. i trusted him, and if he'd said i needed a c-section i would have gone with that whether i'd wanted to or not - childbirth is full of risks and curveballs, and that's why we have experts like him to give us their best bet.

dr brennan's connection to lenox hill hospital is also a major drawcard. the staff are extremely supportive and professional, and that was so important since i was only allowed one support person (because of corona). a few days after my birth i had to go to the er at a brooklyn hospital on a non-birth related matter, and the staff were horrific - cold, unprofessional, no ppe, and the only way i got through that was because dr brennan coordinated with the er doctors (and calmed me down!). 

post-partem, the brennans have also been incredible. they have seen me by zoom, and started me on treatment on magnetic chair that gives a bajillian pelvic floor exercises in a short amount of time - well worth it!

i was horrified to read a review that dr brennan is a 'yeller' and jais tries to cover up - what bizarre accusations. nothing could be further from the truth. dr brennan is calm, kind, and nothing is too difficult. jais is also a delight - hilarious and incredibly supportive. they are cautious but not overzealous with testing, and they never pressured me - eg i decided not to get the amnio or the late term scans, and there was never any pressure to do the contrary. i was bemused by the reviewer who questioned the regular internal and external ultrasounds - how do you think dr brennan is supposed to see what's going on? holistic fortune-telling? x-ray vision? psychic ability? (side note: i loved these ultrasounds - hearing my baby's heart beat each week was the most incredible part of pregnancy. why would anyone not want that??) 

thank you, dr brennan and jais, for being with me on this remarkable journey. if i have another baby i want you by my side again every step of the way!

my advice to this hospital is that they speak to the family member that brought the patient in so that they can get a complete medical history, including medications (which i had to convince the nurse with attitude to take a copy of). they have no idea what i remember compared to my husband because i've lived through his issues and have clarity as to what happened in the past. to think that i may risk life to travel to loma linda to get proper care upsets me.  it's pathetic.

i am beyond happy i went to dr. kim for my surgery. he's very straight to the point, nice, and attentive. pre op i was a 32b, i haven't been able try on different bras because of this pandemic, but i'm assuming i'm a 32 d or dd. i went under the muscle with my incision under my breast. i got high profile 415cc silicone implants. this is going to be a long review about my whole 90 day journey.  the first week was hard but everyday got better and better, trust me it's so worth it. i am extremely pleased with my results and i allowed dr. kim to pick the size that would best suit my body type and lifestyle (i am a very active person). 


day of surgery (day one)
- waking up from surgery feeling a lot of pressure. first words waking up "wow they weren't kidding about the amount of pressure you feel".
- feeling very "drunk" nauseous, dizzy, on the verge of vomiting. feeling lasted 3 hours post op.
- ate soups, apple sauce, yogurt, and bread
- no pain, just a lot of pressure and soreness
- in and out of sleep all day
- needed help taking pants off to use the toilet
days 2-5 post op
- more movement, can pants off to use toilet
- felt very out of it from medication, in and out of sleep everyday
- ate my first meals (small healthy meals)
- had yogurt with every antibiotic
- no bowel movement until day 5
- washed lower body on day 4
- last norco was early morning day 5
- minimal arm movement
- no pain, a lot of soreness
- day 4 less chest pressure
- whole body felt tender (side effects from anesthesia)
- very bloated for a whole week (looked 6 months pregnant)
day 6-10 
- day 6, no more pain killers (only antibiotic), pains here and there, a lot of soreness, less pressure.
- clear mind and less naps after stopping norco 
- lower back/butt pain from sleeping sitting up 
- pain that felt like a bruised rib on lower left boob
- more movement with arms, can't lift above shoulders
- drove on day 7
- normal bowel movements
- 1 week post op. tape removal was a little painful but satisfying. stitches were easy to remove without pain (strange sensation). regarding pain under left boob doctor said it was an inflamed blood vessel. should heal within a week. 
- still a lot of swelling on the top
- started massage, breast feel very tender and sore when preforming. 30-40 mins a day
- feeling better everyday
- first night given the okay to sleep flat on back (slept with two pillows below my head, two pillows beside each hip. slept good). 
day 11-14
- no pain
- mild tenderness under left boob
- can lift arms above head on day 14
- dry skin on breasts
- itchy
- nipples extremely sensitive since day 1
day 60 
- no pain
- nipples no longer sensitive 
- area below nipples still slightly numb 
day 90
- normal sensation on left nipple, right nipple slightly numb, both breast slightly numb around incision. 
- massaging everyday 30-45 mins.
- no pain or discomfort.

there is so much to say about this place but my perceptions were colored by the covid19 outbreak. we had a monday appointment for emergency surgery and arrived early. we parked across the street from the hospital and had to pay for parking for the day because i did not receive any previous notice to use the valet parking they provide or one of the other lots that are apparently theirs. the one we parked in belongs to the other hospital but there was nothing to let us know and they do not work together. i was only told after we had entered to check-in. 
because of covid 19 they had heightened security and were limiting visitors. they also handled all the check-ins with no contact. when we checked in they had us wait and then needed our dr's information as they did not have it on file. there was some trouble finding them in the computer but when they did they had us wait some more. we were then informed that the insurance had denied coverage of the surgery and they had their insurance department working on it. when they hit a brick wall they had us go to emergency to check in to expedite the insurance approval. after doing this we were sent to the dr for an exam to determine exactly what would have to be done. 

we had the exam and were told that we had to wait 48 hours, instead of 7 to 10 days, for the insurance to approve the surgery. we had to drive back to orlando and drive back down the following day for surgery to take place on wednesday. on tuesday we got word for the time to check-in and that we would be seeing the dr for a follow-up on thursday morning. when we arrived wednesday morning early they were shutting down their valet parking and they directed us to a parking lot we could park in for free. at the lot they told us we would have to pay for parking on the way out. we went to the hospital and check-in went smoothly for the surgery. only one person was allowed to accompany any patient so it was fairly empty. they were checking everyone at the door on the way in and anyone having symptoms could not enter. 

for our part the surgery was long but we were told it went very well. the dr came out and spoke to me after and was very pleasant. towards the end of recovery i was able to join my child and wait with them till it was time to leave. when we were ready to go they sent me to get the car and said they would bring them down to me. i got our vehicle and drove back to the front where the security told me to call for them to bring them down. i explained that they did not give me a number and said they would be right down. they begrudgingly let me wait where others were already being allowed to wait. they were down quickly and were helped into our vehicle. on thursday we arrived early and my other child was with us as we had checked out of the hotel. i had my kids get out and stand outside while i parked the car. when i came over they had gotten the one who had surgery a wheelchair and i switched places with my youngest and gave them directions to the car. they had to walk there alone in the dark while took car of the one who had surgery. security was brusk and did not care that a minor would be walking alone on the streets and waiting in a car in an unsecured or guarded parking lot.

the appointment went well and they were happy with the look of the eye. we had to stay for well over an hour to see if they could get the pressure down but we left with them satisfied and an appointment with our local specialist on monday. on our way out security and police were escorting someone out that was being a disturbance. 

overall we were extremely satisfied with the doctors and administrative staff we dealt with. they worked very hard to get everything done and performed a good surgery. my only issues were with security and the dissemination of information to all the employees in a timely manner. they also did a poor job informing patients of how everything worked and basics like where to park. 

if you need work on an eye this is a great place to get service but ask a lot of questions in advance especially if you have to travel to get service here.
