i'm about 10 weeks out from birth and feel like i'm finally ready to review birth day presence. 
first of all, i'm really glad businesses like this exist to support women/families as they grow and i feel like i got some solid information at the two classes i attended (newborn care/lactation and birthing/labor). i also sensed that the instructors genuinely cared about their work and really wanted us to walk away with good, usable information. 
so why only 3 stars? i just didn't have that wow moment. while i got some decent information i felt like a lot of it was very available in books/online for a fraction of the cost and frankly, there was so much we didn't cover. birth and postpartum are obviously extremely variable but i couldn't use any of the information or tips they gave me at the birthing class. like, none of it. i wondered if my labor/birth was so odd but when i told other women my experience some of them had similar labors so it's not like i was a big outlier or anything. 
as far as newborn care has gone, some of the stuff i learned in the class has been valuable but for the most part i just had to get in there, use my instincts and learn on my own. people make a big deal about changing diapers but it's been pretty self explanatory (just don't get peed on if you have a boy : p).
what's more, the space is small and stuffy/cramped which is not ideal with a room full of pregnant people and their partners. 
i had also signed up for an infant cpr class and couldn't attend due to covid19 but they've been gracious about offering us an online makeup when we're ready. 
all of this said, birth day presence has different classes and module set ups to try and accommodate people's schedules and are connected with boober which connects families to doulas, lactation consultants etc which is also very needed. customer service has been great if a little slow at times.
i guess i learned that i'm not one for birthing classes and more of a do it yourself kinda girl? i didn't take any classes elsewhere so i have nothing to compare it to but these guys came highly recommended from like everyone including my doctor. based on the other ratings, not everyone had this experience so if you really want a birthing class and don't want to do it at a hospital i'm sure this is a good choice. just didn't wow me.

i had an annual membership at this massage envy.  i don't love the corporate environment and frequent attempts to sell me more services and products, but i found a massage therapist i liked and had monthly 90 minute massages at a cost of the monthly $65 charge for membership, plus $23 additional for the 90 minute massage.  at the end of 2019, i asked a massage envy employee who worked at the front desk when my membership was terminating and how i would turn off auto-renew for my account at the end of my membership.  the employee told me that the last monthly charge for my account would occur in february 2020, and i'd get one last massage after that charge went through.  she said she would turn off auto-renew on my account, to take effect after the february 2020 charge to my credit card. i repeated this back to her at the end of the conversation to make sure that i understood what she said. 
i scheduled a massage last sunday (march 15), and when i checked out, the employee behind the desk charged my card $143 + tip.  i explained the history and, after, she researched my account, she told me that the employee who said that my last membership charge would be in february was wrong and that the february date in their system actually referred to the auto-renewal date.  i don't recall how she said their system worded that date, but it sounded like it was an easy mistake to make.  i told her i didn't expect to pay $143 for the massage and she said she couldn't do anything.  i asked about speaking to a manager, and the employee gave me a card with an email address to use to contact the manager (who apparently wasn't there).
i sent a message to the generic email address i was given explaining what happened and asking that they refund the difference between the $143 price i was charged and the monthly membership rate of $88.  i received a prompt reply from an anonymous person.  he/she/it apologized for the employee's mistake in giving me bad information and refused to refund any money.  offered me a free "enhancement" on my next service.  are you kidding me?  you massively overcharged me for a massage that i never would have scheduled if i had been given the correct information by your employee when i asked about my termination date, and you think i'm going to get another treatment at your establishment?  this management/location is profiting off of their own employee's mistake, which is unconscionable on so many levels.  yes, the coronavirus is hitting all of us hard right now, but customers shouldn't be treated this way, especially when your employee made the mistake that led to the overcharge.
please don't support this location of massage envy.

so i started to develop a sore throat late wednesday night, just on my left side. i also started to get the chills & increase in temp. but i had some gi issues going on after eating take out about 6 hrs prior, so i wasn't sure if the chills & increase of temp was related to my stomach issue (gi). thursday my left tonsil  started to enlarge & late that night i spiked a temp. & started to feel like crap. friday am i kept waking up as if i was having trouble swallowing so i looked @ my throat & now my right tonsil was swollen & both were sore. there was some white spots back there too. 

i have had strep before & figured that was what was going on. i have a pmd but he's a good drive & always like an hour or longer wait because he is always running behind. when i'm not feeling good i'm not in the mood to drive far or wait forever for treatment.  

as an er nurse my swollen tonsils & me wanting to rule out strep throat is not an appropriate visit to an er plus it would cost me a lot of money. i have used cvs minute clinics in the past & they're reasonably priced. i unfortunately don't have health insurance right now as i work per diem (no benefits) so i wanted to go somewhere not too expensive & some place i wouldn't have to wait hours at. 

if you go on yelp & do a search for cvs minute clinics & put in your zip code ones will show up close to your zip code. unfortunately this location wasn't inside the cvs close to my house that i go to. that one had a wait, this one had no wait. 

few things to know. they say they're closed 1:30pm-2:30pm because they go to lunch. well they could open after 2:30pm if they get to lunch late due to their last patient that they see prior going to lunch. the app. will not tell you if they're @ lunch. when i looked @ the app. it said there was no wait time. you can sign up on-line to "hold your spot" so when i did it @ first it put in the time that it was & it said to get there within 5 minutes of your appt. time to sign in on their kiosk. i had to cancel my appt. because i was still at home & it was about a 7-10 minute drive. i waited till i got closer to the store then signed up. parked & went inside. 

as i was signing in on the kiosk the np had seen me & mentioned to me that she was going to lunch & wouldn't be back for a 1/2 hr. it was a little after 3pm. she had a put a sticky note down on the table stating that but i didn't see it cause i went right for the computer screen. 

she had told me the website doesn't tell you when they go to lunch or get back. she told me the clinic on lv blvd didn't have a wait & i said "by the time i get there you'll be back from lunch." so i told her i would just wait. due to the coronavirus & us having to "social distance" i was told to wait in my car or outside & she said she would call me when she got back from lunch. she did this exactly. the wait was 1/2hr. 

when she had called me she had asked me why i was coming in as they need to screen before letting you come back inside. 

her name was lisa, np (nurse practitioner). she was very nice, professional, didn't rush me & listened to all my symptoms. did a through triage. i was hoping that just by my symptoms & my throat i could just get treated for strep cause another cvs minute clinic has done that in the past. she told me that they can't do that but they can do a rapid strep right there & i would get my results in 2 minutes. this was an additional cost. i was hoping for some steroids to help with the swelling but there they have a protocol where they won't prescribe steroids for this. er's will, maybe not all but some of them do. 

so i was debating on whether or not to get the strep test because if it came back negative, which it can & my swollen tonsils could have just been a viral problem & we don't take antibiotics for virus's, we treat the symptoms. i would have walked out of there as miserable as i was when i walked in. being seen for a "sickness" & strep test was about $170 which i thought was very expensive. mind you i was a "cash" paying patient. so i decided just to do it. i tell ya something....i never wanted a strep test to come back positive as i did today!! lol

well it came back positive for strep. we discussed antibiotics that she could prescribe to see if i've been on them before & had no issues as i have 2 allergies to antibiotics. she also offered to write for some liquid lidocaine for me to gargle to help numb the pain. i probably was with her in the private room, with door closed for apx. 45 minutes. she was able to send my rx's to the pharmacy next door & they will fill those over people coming in with new rx or refills so that was cool. less waiting. 

check their website out before going to see if what you want to be seen for is something they can do. it's probably cheaper & quicker then an urgent care & def. is vs an er visit.

expecting mama's; look no further.

i am a first time mother and was recommended to have jo as my midwife by a friend of a friend. before i met her, she was described to me as a "evidence-based, holistic, calming, smart, caring, feminist midwife," exactly what i wanted. i am a registered nurse, so i am pretty well versed in what is out there as far as care-providers go, and i knew i wanted someone who was going to take into account the whole picture and not just the sum of my body parts (like most ob-gyns tend to do). 

next thing i know, i am having a phone consult with what feels like someone who is already my fierce advocate and friend. fast-forward to the first in-person appointment in her very chic private office (which is a beautifully decorated bright and airy space; it's extremely calming). there are books with the theme of empowering women in pregnancy and childbirth strewn all over the waiting room, which feels more like a living room that i am just chilling out in before my medical appointment. i actually never really felt like i was in an austere medical environment, though her office is set up as a fully functioning prenatal clinic. i never sat in her waiting room with another patient. it always felt like a prenatal visit with jo was just catching up with her on what was going on in my life with a side of some tests and exams. every visit was more calming than the last, i really breezed right through my pregnancy in the most zen state of mind and i have jo to thank for that because she can attest to the fact that my life was literally in a crazy chaotic state throughout the entire 10 months!! 

now for the important part...my birth!! it was the most extraordinary experience of my life. whenever i tell my birth story i start by saying i had the most incredible team around me, and that is what made the difference. jo came to my house when i was in labor to check how dilated i was because i didn't want to be in the hospital until the last minute. that might have been an added bonus because of the whole covid-19 situation but it is just an example of how above and beyond she went for me. once we were in the hospital, i labored there for about 3.5 hours and jo never left my side. she coached me through the hardest parts of the labor process and skillfully talked me out of an epidural i was screaming for at 8cm because she knew that it was a goal of mine to have a natural birth. i am sure many other providers would have just let me give up but she expertly danced a fine line between talking me out of it, while also taking my pain seriously and allowing me the option of relief if i needed it. 

tldr; look no further for a midwife. prenatal zen-ness and a magical birth experience, despite being in the middle of an insane pandemic!

it's important that we support our local businesses during this covid19 crisis and spread the word about those that are going the extra mile. 

5nbc dfw morning news: antibody testing could help north texans learn if they already recovered from coronavirus by larry collins. "the antibodies test is a finger-prick test that you can draw a little bit of blood," sneha patel with metroplex medical centres said. "usually within 15 minutes, we will get a negative/positive for each of the antibodies." 5nbc dfw news report. metroplex medical centres will offer the testing in fort worth, dallas and plano starting friday, april 17.

we are so grateful that metroplex medical centres was offering the covid-19 rapid testing in our area. 

it was easy to make a reservation but by the time i got to the website they were sold out with two spots left for saturday. i signed up because i have had symptoms for 3 weeks. i signed up my 19 y/o daughter who is autoimmune compromised from lupus, fibro, and rheumatoid arthritis but has had no symptoms. 
 
the plano event was a one day only, by appointment only, no walk-ins allowed, only cars for drive-thru. the drive-thru, the symbol of american excess, or efficiency, is now the means by which many are being tested for the coronavirus. they had an organized event professionally set up in the parking lot. we were instructed not to open the windows unless asked to do so. stay in the car and don't get out unless asked to do so. our results would be text to us. 

once we arrived there was a check-in point (you have to have your reservation paperwork) and they collected $20.00 cash (no insurance or additional payment required). 

next, you pulled around the building and visited with a healthcare person who pricked your finger. the whole process for both of us took less than 10 minutes. they tell you to stay nearby for your test results because you might need to come back and be tested for the covid19 virus. 

we waited for approximately 20 minutes. i got a text saying i was negative. but my daughter tested igg positive. this means she had covid19 at some point but is now in a convalescent recovering state. we were shocked to get this news that she has the antigen. 

see .. she's that one person you hear who has covid19 but no symptoms. 

this was an eye opening experience!

second: you will be waiting in your car, so i wouldn't recommend bringing children since the wait is long, and as we go into hotter weather, this is bound to be problematic.
third: i think they are still trying to work all the kinks out to make this a smoother process, but i'm sure there are obstacles that even they aren't aware of yet, so give them room to do what they have to do and be patient. 
as it gets hotter, this process is going to really suck. just try to be prepared and allow them to do their jobs under difficult circumstances.

during covid-19, right after the travel ban, i was on quarantine for 14 days since i arrived from europe on vacation.  during that time, i fell ill and after a few days under virtual care, my doctor advised me to go to the er.  i chose memorial hermann sugar land thinking i would get good care.  i was totally wrong.

once in the er, which was set up efficiently because of the virus, the er doctor immediately explained to me that they will not send my covid-19 test off to be tested unless i was admitted to the hospital.  his main concern was not diagnosing my problem but explaining that i would have to go somewhere else to get tested for covid-19.

i was advised to go the the er by my doctor because i was coughing excessively, barely able to breath, experiencing pain in my back when breathing and coughing, wheezing and extreme shortness of breath even with using an inhaler.  my temp stayed below 100.4 so it wasn't considered a fever.

the er began to run tests:  chest x-rays, ct scan, urine-analysis, blood-work, i.v., etc.

i waited about 45 minutes for all the test results to return and during that time, i suffered and tried to breath over and over in spite of the difficulties i was experiencing.  finally, the er doctor returned (dr. b. parker) and said that my lungs were clear and that the covid-19 swab would not be sent to the lab because i'm not being admitted to the hospital.  i stated that i understood about the swab but i didn't understand what was going on with my breathing so i asked him again about my lungs.  dr. parker repeated that my lungs were "all clear" and that there was no sign of the virus in my lungs. 

i asked the doctor what was he diagnosing me as having. since we know there's no sign of covid-19 in my lungs, what is it then and what was he going to give me to help me breath.   dr. parker turned the paper around and it read, "cough - adult".  i asked, "so you're diagnosing me as having a cough?"  he replied yes.  i was dumbfounded.  i came to the er with a cough and shortness of breath and now the dr. was telling me that i had a cough.  wow!  

i asked him what was he going to do about helping me?  he stated that he was calling in prescriptions to my pharmacy to take but to act like i had covid-10 and still isolate.  he stated that he believed it was just an allergy infection and that these meds would clear it up.  i informed him that i don't typically suffer with allergies and that i had been taking zyrtec because the virtual doctor i spoke to recommended it but i wasn't getting any better.  he reemphasized again that the test would not be sent and that if i wanted a covid-19 test, i needed to go to another site.  i asked about an antibiotic to clear up the infection and he said the meds he prescribed would clear up the infection.  i later learned that the meds were regular over-the-counter stuff that i had already been using that wasn't effective:  tylenol, mucinex and claritin-d.

i believe dr. parker's only concern was covid-19 and not finding the real source of my problems.  i asked my discharge nurse again about my lungs being "all clear" and she said well they are not all clear and that they had a haze over them.  i asked what does a haze mean.  she informed me that the doctor believes the haze is possibly from a bacteria infection from allergies so he's prescribed some meds to help.  i again said i don't suffer with allergies but ok the pollen is high so i guess.  

i was discharged and walked to my car still struggling to breath just the same way as i walked into the hospital.   

that was saturday, march 21st. fast forward to wednesday, march 25th and i was not feeling any better, in fact, i felt worse. i called my doctor both the 25th and 26th and left messages. her nurse called my back on the 27th and informed me to stop taking all allergy meds immediately and that she had reviewed the labs and x-rays and they believe that haze over my right lung is pneumonia.

pneumonia?!!  so i had pneumonia in the right lung for an additional 6 days without any treatment?!  why would dr. parker say i was "all clear" and ignore the haze?  i had to take additional time from work to heal whereas if dr. parker would have just taken the time to explore my results for something more than covid-19, he could have treated me correctly and i could have returned back to work without taking additional time.  

lastly, once i got the bill, i saw that i was billed $273.50 for a pregnancy test!!!  the admitting nurse asked if there was anyway i could be pregnant, i immediately answered no and explained why i couldn't be.  so why would you give me, a 49 yr old woman with a valid reason a pregnancy test?  especially for $273.50.  over billing???   yes!

i will never go back to memorial hermann sugar land emergency room.  the care of the treating physician was below sub-par and i could have saved way more time and money going to another facility.

i had an excellent experience with pivot. after years of chronic illness, in 2019 i was finally able to exercise and hike again. so when i suffered a major injury a few months in, it seemed at first like a big setback. but working with lindsay gave me the strength and confidence to see that i could make major steps forward, and even come out stronger than before i was injured. 

i injured my legs in late summer 2019 on a hike, and spent fall recovering on doctor's orders. when i was ready for pt, i checked out three pt options in the neighborhood, including pivot which a friend had recommended years ago when she had a good rehab experience. 

i suffer from chronic migraines and most pt places are brightly lit with glaring overhead lights, which is bad news for me. pivot has this kind of setup, but the director danielle showed me how i could use a therapy table with a curtain and another one away from an overhead, to give me options that would work for me. she was helpful and supportive, and helped me check out the facility before scheduling. both danielle and lindsay are great. i scheduled with lindsay due to availability. 

lindsay evaluated me and started me on a program. we worked together from late december through february, and she re-evaluated me multiple times. with chronic pain, it's hard for me to figure out how to answer pain scale questions that are important for evaluation, and she always helped walk me through my questions. the program she created was varied and fun. it felt great to be able to clearly measure how i was progressing by using stronger resistance, heavier weights, moving to higher intensity and so on. and when i came up against issues, she helped me to proceed in a safe way that was finely tuned to other physical challenges i navigate, like clicking from my joints.

by the time i was ready to graduate, not only did i make a full recovery, i felt stronger than when i was injured, and ready to move up to a regular strength training program. she also gave me all the advice, printouts, online videos, and recommendations that enabled me to achieve what i wanted to achieve in rehab.   

important to note: seeing a great physical therapist is about 20% of the work. people who recover as well as i did continually put in the effort to follow an increasingly difficult program. athletes and regular gym-goers are used to following a regimen. i had been dealing with chronic illness for years and hadn't been in good enough health for regular exercise until early 2019. but i put in the work to follow lindsay's program and build back up.

(coronavirus p.s.: i made the bad-timing choice of joining a gym in feb 2020 as i was wrapping pt... but i made it there consistently for 11 sessions. then one day i found myself listening to early podcasts about flattening the curve when few people were taking it seriously. and there i was... at the gym... i left, stocked up on groceries, and hunkered down at home before march hit. thanks to my practice with lindsay, i had a mini-home gym ready to go and was well-equipped going into a long time staying safe at home.)

i've had no response at all to the letter i mailed them so here's the information for anyone who might be considering this place.
***************************************************************

i cannot express too adamantly my dismay at the shortcomings of your facilities, staff training, test structure, and cleanliness.  each of these problems is readily resolved with a patient-centered focus and/or a trip to home depot so i am taking the trouble of listing them for you. 

re facilities
* patients can only get staff attention by, literally, sitting up in bed and waving their arms indefinitely.  a simple buzzer or alexa system of some sort is essential.  i waved in bed for several minutes, turned on the bed lamp, waved some more, got out bed, waved some more, tried to find some core plug for the leads to avoid pulling them out, pulled off all my leads, used the restroom, walked down the hall, and found the attendant who still had no idea i needed attention!

* patients have no access to temperature control, a factor that certainly impacts sleep.  since expense probably prohibits retrofitting temperature controls for each room, patients need a set of resources to make such adjustments as are possible.  a low-noise fan with varying controls and blankets of varying weights are minimally required.  knowing about this situation prior to testing, gives patients an opportunity to pack robes and so on appropriately

* patients have incomplete light control, a matter that the head-leads make impossible to resolve with a sleep mask.  since any substantive changes are likely to be too expensive, a few low-cost changes should help, including overhead lamps with multi-level settings that can be reached easily.  the small lights on the can tv be covered with something as simple as index cards for those who need it.

* the rooms are not soundproof which means that a neighbor's snoring, television, or the attendant's cell phone conversations can easily disrupt a patient's efforts to sleep.  a white noise machine would be of some use.



re staff training
* attendants need to check patients' tv monitor screens frequently.  

* staff need to learn how to keep their voices down when they must talk on their phones.  closing that door and speaking from the back of the room in a quiet voice would help.

* heavy use of cologne or perfume should be prohibited, including the morning sessions.  

* evening attendants need to know enough about the napping-test schedules to ensure that vital medicines will be available exactly when prescribed.  medication timing can sometimes be adjusted if patients have the opportunity to work with well-informed staff on the matter.  it's impossible to plan for daytime medication schedules when nighttime staff have no knowledge about the napping-test procedures.



re test structure
* patients are required to wake up at 5:30 a.m. because it suits the staff schedule.  waking people who must for their jobs or other obligations is certainly appropriate.  waking up everyone, however, is not.  the priorities need to be, in this order, sufficiently accurate test data, patient needs, staffing convenience.

* the napping-test procedure requires transparency.  it might be set based on staffing schedules, patient data, a pre-set pattern, or something else entirely.  nothing is provided or available to inform patients.



re cleanliness
* upon entering the site, patients have no signage directing them to virus-protection resources.  

* a clean, uncluttered counter should hold a professional sign on contacting the attendant.  

* gloves and masks should be clearly offered for patient use. 

* a statement regarding the company's means of and commitment to addressing virus-protection should be available.

* bathrooms should have soap.

* hand towels need to be newly set out; none should be wrinkled enough to indicate prior use.

* since patients shouldn't be wearing gloves to bed, cleaning wipes should be available for wiping off doorknobs, light switches, and other surfaces that are likely to be touched by patients who rub their faces in the night, get up, and return to bed.

* staff should wear masks at all times.  

* staff need to change gloves or use sanitizer in sight of the patients, particularly when handling phones and moving between patients.

- my grandma ended up passing away april 6th, when her oxygen levels dropped. the day before they had called and said she was steady and eating again with her fever gone. before that, we had been unable to reach anyone for four days with another update since we weren't able to visit when they told us they'd call with daily updates. i really do understand and empathize with the staff, as many also got sick and they probably didn't have enough people working.. but on the other hand, my family and i were very worried about our grandma. being promised daily updates and then not hearing anything multiple days really gave us a ton of anxiety. 
- before they closed and the outbreak had started in wa already, my dad came to visit with a mask out of precaution. the staff there were shocked and asked him if he was sick. none of them were wearing any masks, and when i heard this i was very disappointed but also not surprised an outbreak had started at the facility.
- they are not being transparent with their numbers. when the outbreak started at the facility, the website last stated 26 residents and 16 staff had been diagnosed before changing to a generic "we are following all guidelines" statement. they took off how many have passed or been diagnosed - i'm sure it's a lot more! i have told my family friends and they've all freaked out and had similar experiences with their relatives living in this facility. see statement here: https://cristaseniorliving.org/crista-senior-living-covid-19-response/

regardless of these faults, i do acknowledge above that the staff was trying their best and there are very difficult circumstances right now. i do appreciate everyone there who had taken care of my grandma over the years she lived there. something that stuck with me was the caretaker who called us when she got diagnosed with the virus to let us know that she was loved and cared for, and it truly sounded like she meant it. i do, however, find issue with upper management and a lot of other things that have occurred over the past few weeks which is why i give this facility two stars.

we arrived at the birth center in the morning, ready to deliver, and before we were admitted, we were told to transfer to a hospital because our baby was breech, (butt down). the main part of the complaint is the size of the refund. we received only a small portion back ($1,750) even though we did not deliver there. 

as a note, we did get back "more" than what was stipulated in the contract if you transfer before birth-related services take place in the birth center. we knew there was a 20% chance this could happen but of course, we thought that wouldn't happen to us. 

we had three prenatal visits - valued at $500, $250, $250, and also took two of their classes two hours tops (lactation class and infant care classes, our est. value $100/ea.) while in labor at home, we talked and text with the on-call midwife who was helpful and had us come in at the right time. this was approximately ten hours, my guess is $130 per hour or $1,300 for that service.

this is our estimate of the expenses. 
$6,500 - total paid for delivery at the birth center.
 -$1,000 - three prenatal visits
 -$1,300 - access to an on-call midwife during at-home labor 
 -$200 - two classes

this is our guess, without being cheap on the cost of services provided. the expected refund should be closer to $4,000, not $1,750.

i want to start by saying i'm a registered nurse and have worked in a hospital for over 11 years. i'm also working in the midst of the current covid19 pandemic. it's stressful right now, i get it. this is my first yelp review and its not intended to bad mouth staff. i do however want to bring this experience to the attention of saint mary's as a way to hopefully prevent the same thing from happening to someone else. i live just outside of sacramento and my 24 year old daughter lives in reno. about two weeks ago she developed some mild symptoms; cough, mild headache, sore throat, minor chest and nasal congestion. early monday morning she suddenly developed chills, fever and shortness of breath. i instructed her to go to the ed. upon arrival, her heart rate was 130 and she had a temp of 100f. a chest xray, ekg, labs and iv fluids were ordered. the flu and strep were ruled out. no covid19 was ordered.
my daughter was released with out anything other than a prescription for zofran (for nausea which she didn't have). the following day, she emailed me her lab results. i was mortified to see her wbc was 19.6!! trained medical professionals will know the significance of this. basically double the high end of normal. i won't bore you with the differentials that further showed something bacterial was most likely going on. with a heart rate of 130, shortness of breath, fever and bp of 106/55 and a white count of 19.6 any rn or md should have been concerned my daughter could be septic. she left your facility without any antibiotics! fortunately i have several friends who are md's and was able to get her a prescription for an antibiotic and an inhaler for a bad case of bronchitis. i'm happy to report she is finally feeling much better. like i said, i'm honestly dumbfounded... again, i understand things are intense and downright "crazy" right now. but to me, this was something that should never have happened. it's also worth mentioning, as a 24 year old young woman, her male nurse, without warning, lifted her shirt to do the ekg without regard for her modesty. she was mortified. i am glad they did it with a heart rate in the 130's but it doesn't take even one extra second to tell your patent what your doing. i wish all my fellow medical staff near and far the best of luck during this unprecedented time! stay well...

i went to four consultations with other ophthalmologists before deciding to move forward with dr. berg. i had been searching since october 2019 and did not make up my mind until february 2020 after extensive research and comparing each facility to decide which one would be best for me. some of them were more affordable but at the end of the day i wasn't shopping for a set of tires, it's my eyes we're talking about. i decided to go with dr. berg because of the customized technology his office had to offer. the equipment at dr. berg's office reads your exact prescription, therefore you get better vision and it corrects other vision problems you may have. i had a very mild prescription and astigmatism. i also had night vision issues such as halos and starburst vision. i was having a lot of problems when driving, the freeway signs bothered me and any sort of reflection or bright light. 

the day of the surgery march 13, 2020 (yes i had my surgery friday 13th because that's how much i trusted dr. berg) i went in for some additional eye testing, dr. berg came in to check up on me a few times and i asked him some additional questions i had. i was prepped for surgery and next thing you know i'm sitting on the surgery table. they gave me medication for anxiety, which honestly didn't do much but i was able to just go through it and i knew it would be worth it at the end. dr. berg made me feel so much better because he talked me through the entire surgery, which kind of distracted me from what was happening because you can't see anything when they lift the cornea flap. the entire surgery took about 10-15 minutes and i was done! i was given a kit with drops, goggles, tape and some sunglasses. i got home around noon took a nap and woke up around 6-7pm and i was feeling great. i even walked outside to get some food and watched tv that night. healing process was quick, i did have some bruising on both of my eyes which went away after 2 weeks. after care isn't that complicated just use common sense and keep your eyes clean, don't wear make up and don't rub your eyes. i have gotten myself into a habit of not touching my face for a few years now so it wasn't a problem for me but use common sense during recovery and keep your eyes moist. get the nighttime systane gel drops if you can (target $16).

i was always treated kindly and with respect by dr. berg and by his entire staff. they accommodated me around my work schedule for all appointments and for the day of the surgery. i was very thankful dr. berg still checked up on me despite the covid-29 situation that we are currently having in los angeles. i highly recommend dr. berg, i was recommended to him by a work colleague and i am so grateful i came across such an amazing eye surgeon. my life has changed for the better, i can see the time when i wake up in the morning. i can watch television without feeling uncomfortable, i can exercise without having to worry about my glasses or contacts, i can see life with clarity. i regret not doing this surgery sooner because i feel like i was missing out before. this has been one of the best investments i've ever made on myself and i couldn't be happier. he checked my vision this week and i now have better than 20/20 vision! i'm still having some halo vision problems at night but that is very common the first few months after surgery. lastly i thought it was really cool how your family can watch the surgery and i was given a cd of my surgery! i hope this review helps you make your decision and remember you can pay for your surgery using fsa (pretax dollars) like i did, so i didn't have to come up with the lump sum to pay for the surgery. if you are reading this dr. berg thank you so much i really appreciate everything you have done for me! i will make sure to tell all my friends and family who the best ophthalmologist in los angeles is!

i realize this is one of those places where your mileage may vary, but it has been a very good fit for my needs. i honestly chose this pt from a list for its convenient location, and got lucky that the therapists are excellent here (i did pt around the corner from here 2 years ago for the same issues and it wasn't good at all). 

regardless of my number of check-ins, i've been coming for months and have logged over a dozen visits. a huge plus is they are open during this whole covid thing, as many of my pain management modalities are closed. they keep the space very clean, and have greatly reduced the number of patients seen per day. 

i love that they tailor my hour to how i feel- if my pain is high, it's more massage, graston method, e-stim and ice. if i feel okay, i get to work on improving my mobility and strengthening my shoulder. i actually subluxed then fully dislocated my shoulder in the midst of coming here, and the therapy here was much more pleasant than going to urgent care (i still have traumatic memories of them yanking my arm the last time it dislocated lol).

they are also very honest. i am fully aware now that i will never be pain-free, but i can manage my inflammation and such with proper diet (yay for my so-called low-carb life!), exercise and meditation/breathing. 

that said, i have learned a lot of exercises and isometric holds, and they even gave me a free app with all the exercises so i can do homework on my own. the app is great- it tracks my pain level and how difficult each exercise is. 

overall, i am truly grateful for this business.

i've had aud (alcohol use disorder) for about 40 years. i've tried everything: hypnosis, acupuncture, years on antabuse, 6 months and then 7 years sober in aa in 2000s. each relapse turned into a several weeks long binge, forcing me to seek help again. finally, in 2014 i discovered sinclair method (https://www.the-sinclair-method.com/), which turned out to be a lifesaver. my drinking quickly went down to safe limits and i started to have alcohol free days several times a week. for 5.5 years i was a social drinker, a "normie" in aa speak - until covid struck. 

i live alone, the lockdown made me seriously depressed. all my routines and nearly all social contacts were broken and it felt like a solitary confinement. at some point in april, i stopped taking my medication as prescribed by the sinclair method. from there, my drinking quickly escalated and turned into a heavy 6 weeks binge. by may 13 i had to go to er and then to a 10 days detox in holister; spent the first night in icu nearly having a heart attack. after i got back home on sunday may 24, i wanted to make sure that sinclaire is still working (i still had some meds left from my last refill); i had 3 drinks on the first day, then it went 1, 1, 0, 1, 0 - amazing, considering my condition before the detox. 

in the meantime, my gf discovered the intensive outpatient program (iop) at good sam behavioral. i was surprised to learn that dr cecil a. bradley, who prescribed me naltrexone all these years, is the medical director of this program. the program seemed very useful since a) it is in person, no zoom, b) i got a double diagnosis and could address my underlying emotional issues and c) i could get an extended medical leave, since i was not feeling up to getting back to work immediately. on thursday, may 28 i was there and talked to marcella (admissions) dr khan (sp? md), nurse diane and some other people. i was very open about what i've been doing before, what brought me there and about my intentions (go back on sinclaire, since it works great and aa stopped working for me at some point). everybody seemed to be open-minded, accepting and approving of my course of treatment. some even wrote down the name of my method and said they were curious and want to learn more about it.

thursday and friday sessions were pretty nice, with meditation, some cbt and open discussions on topics suggested by patients themselves. and then, on friday noon dr bradley showed up, took me to his office and told me that their program is based on full abstinence and if i keep up the  controlled drinking, i have to leave. he said there are alternatives to aa and suggested some other program - he just could remember it's name. he is in his 80s and seems to forget things. i promised to think about it over the weekend and tell him about my decision on monday. after all, at this point i could easily refrain from drinking for the duration of the program.

however, on monday my case manager handed me a recovery plan with mandatory conditions: attend at least 3 meetings a week, find a sponsor and report progress at each morning session. i told her i don't do aa, and i was told to go talk to dr bradley, and again he gave me a dilemma: full abstinence and meetings or leave the program. "there is this other program - can't remember it's name... rational recovery?" "- smart recovery?" "- yes, this must be it". "- i researched it, and it has about the same success rate as aa - which is in single digits - whereas sinclair method has success rate near 80%". "- i don't care. this program requires full abstinence and meetings". so i informed him that i'm quitting and went home.

there are several things that really upset and anger me. 
1) why did dr bradley prescribe my medicine all these years and even wrote me another 3 refills on that monday if he disapproves on sinclair method so much? 
2) how does a doctor refer a patient to some program the name of which he can't even remember? does he know anything about it? or he just doesn't care?
3) why did they admit me at all, knowing full well my intentions, knowing dr bradley's views and giving me false hopes? 
4) what kind of doctors put a patient into completely unscientific, faith-based programs with abysmal success rate and force him to abandon something that is proven to work for 80% and this patient in particular?

so i googled dr bradley and discovered that the medical board of california twice has suspended his license, once in 1990 and second time in 2007 (5 years probation). he also was known to be sending referrals to and working at a couple of shady rehabs ran by an uncertified drug addict.

makes you wonder, how does a doctor like cecil bradley ends up a medical director at well-respected hospital like good sam? i would not recommend going to good sam in- or outpatient behavioral programs until they replace him. the rest of staff seems to be ok, but there is nothing they could do to help me under current leadership.

      when we got to the main hospital, things just went downhill. we pulled up to the door and a nurse told him to just drop me off and they would call him. we tried to convey the reasoning for him to remain but were ignored. an orderly came with a wheelchair and asked why i was there. i tried to explain, but he said " really? cause you look fine!". 
     registered at the desk and was put in a room. guy from registration came in to get my info and for me to sign consent. i was wearing a mask the whole day up to this time. not one person at this point had one on. the registration gentleman brought over my papers to sign, and began flipping the various forms for me by licking his finger! no wonder there's have been confirmed cases at this hospital! 
     then, doctor micheal mai came in, he was masked and gloved.  but as soon as he spoke, i knew nothing was going to get better. i called my boy friend as planned, so he could voice his observations. we were both talked over, the symptoms down played, and he too said "you don't look sick now, though." we were both adamant that this wasn't something to brush off with all of my health problems. in an exasperated tone, we were told " to make us happy he'd run every test under the sun" . when he left my room, he began talking in an extremely loud voice and said ( there were other patients in the rooms on that hall) '" we'll run everything, to rule out the nothing that's wrong with her".

     i've never been treated like a  hypochondriac, especially since they knew nothing about my medical history. total disregard for me as a patient with those inherent rights you hear about totally ignored, as well as contempt when a snap decision on their part was contested. i will assure you, not only will i and my loved ones never patronize this hospital, but i will be posting on social media and  by word of mouth how horribly i was treated. never again.

as for the treatments themselves: i went to the clinic in desperation as kind of a last resort to hopefully avoid what would have been my third suicide attempt and i was not going to get another attempt wrong. after just three infusions people began to say i looked like a different person. they still say that a year later.

i did go back for a round of boosters in december after 37 weeks. not because i needed it or because i was doing poorly but i was going through some things and i was determined to get boosters before i really needed them rather than regret waiting too long. since january 1, i've had three significant blows in my life. then the pandemic happened and everyone is battling with the effects of that. i'm not sure i could have endured anything 2020 has thrown at me had i not got to kcla. but i did. and i'm still going strong.

one is it's like i have a foam pit or a soft place to land when life knocks me down. before, the big blows would hit so hard that i didn't want to get up anymore because it hurt so much and really, why bother getting up when you know you'll be knocked down again and that one will probably be even worse? now, i still get knocked down, but it's so much easier to get back up and get back in the fight.

the other thing is that i feel more freedom. the depression also came with a feeling of oppression. i skipped events and experiences because i couldn't get myself to face them - even if it was something i'd probably enjoy and with people i liked to be around. even worse were the times when i went to those experiences but still missed out because the depression suffocated me and restrained me.

now i'm not carrying all the weight of the depression so my enjoyment is not held back. i can't even tell you how many times i've found myself feeling really happy. it's not all the time, but i'm still surprised by it. i never had a clue people could have moments like this. and even if others had them, there was no chance i would ever have them.

ketamine changed my life. it might change yours too. but definitely contact ketamine clinics of los angeles first when you're ready.

for those worried about the health and safety of their small infants, beware. 

while the office is taking some precautions during covid-19, there are gaps in their processes that made my wife and i extremely uncomfortable during our child's check-up. 

1) receptionists are not required to wear face coverings. the receptionist's windows and doors are both open to the lobby and back hallways resulting in very little protection for infants coming through the front doors.  there are at least 6 receptionists in the office.
2) this is the first medical office we have visited, or heard of, that does not require face coverings to be worn by patients (in this case guardians, as children should not be wearing coverings over their face). the manager shared and stated clearly that they cannot expect everyone to have their own covering, and that they cannot supply a mask to everyone who comes in without one.  other pediatricians in the area do require face coverings, and are supplying 'how-to's' for creating face coverings using everyday materials. 
3) during the check-up our child came into close contact (less than 6 feet, and in one case as little as 2 feet) of three other guardians without face coverings. being in a confined space with complete strangers during this period in time is, in my eyes, inexplicable. if face-coverings were required, then this situation would have been uncomfortable, but understandable.  

my expectation of medical facilities is to provide safety and well-being above all else. i perceive that the current rules and processes indicate that management is more concerned with cost-savings and fear of losing business if forced to turn away a patient may not want to comply with wearing a face-covering. if you feel similarly, you may want to consider getting an update from the office on their current processes or finding another pediatrician that has them in place. 

these concerns and feedback have been shared with the manager as of 6/2/2020.  i am hopeful that the office will make changes to their rules and processes that support the safety and well-being of all their patients. 

although not the focus of this post, we do enjoy our visits with dr. gronberg, and believe him to be a good pediatrician. given a different set of circumstances we likely would have continued visiting him for many years.

my family needs four chaplains to be honest about my grandmother's care during this covid-19 pandemic. she was born in september of 1918, during the 1918 flu pandemic. she grew up in pittsburgh, one of four daughters. she married a union man and lived in livonia for much of her life, where she raised 9 smart, headstrong, and sassy kids -- no easy feat. the union kept her and her husband busy until the tragic, unsolved death of her husband. but she kept going. she kept her family together. she kept herself together. she found comfort in her faith, in the catholic church. she put herself through college in her 60s, studying gerontology. she taught herself piano. she gardened, she played with her grandkids and -- later -- her great-grandkids. she moved to the south, where she played tennis and traded her buick for a purple vw bug. her house was struck by lightning one march, burning many of her keepsakes -- photos, quilts, tokens and trinkets of her life. she kept going, rebuilding on the foundation. she lived to be 80. she loved classic films, gin and liverpool rummy, and defeating any challenger at scrabble. then 90. she moved back to michigan, to be closer to more of her children, to have more support as age caught up. she outlived her sisters, one of her children. she turned 100. then 101.

given the information four chaplains and parent company nexcare health systems has shared with my family, it appears that decided that the opportunity for corporate profit outweighs clear communication of a care plan for my grandmother. it appears they have volunteered to bring covid-19 patients into the care facility where my grandmother lives. four chaplains, in westland, is forcing its staff and residents into a terrible and dangerous situation, where they will share space and breath with people suffering from covid-19 and the residents they work to support. while we should be doing all we can to help people suffering during this pandemic, i do not think it should be at the expense of some of the most vulnerable and long-lived among us. we should also not force people into a situation where they may spread the virus, to their loved ones and the people they so kindly and generously take care of.
nexcare informed us of this decision easter morning, though we have learned from others that not everyone was informed. they told us that they had to do this, that it was required of them by the mandate of governor whitmer. we have not been able to see or speak with my grandmother for weeks, as the facility has been on lockdown to mitigate the spread of the virus. we have seen what the virus can do at nursing homes around the country -- in livonia, seattle, nyc. there is not even a window we can see her through, to show her that we are still here, that we love her, that we have not abandoned her. but to tell us that we cannot see our grandmother because of this virus, and then to move people who are actively infected with this virus into her facility doesn't make sense. they have told us she is listless, despondent. we fear she won't make it through this -- that the isolation and proximity to illness will be too much. nexcare says that there is nothing they can do, they have sentenced my grandmother to this fate. our family is left wondering - if she dies, will we be allowed in? no one knows, and nexcare isn't giving us any clarity.

when i got to kaka'ako's clinical labs of hawai'i, i stopped 6' from the entrance where i was greeted by a nurse.  i stated my business for being there which was for a blood draw rather than needing to see a physician in their clinic.  she asked me several questions to see if i had been exposed to or was experiencing covid-19 symptoms.  when all of my answers were negative, i allowed her to take my temperature with her no touch instant read thermometer gun.  she then opened the door for me to enter the clinic as i handed my insurance cards, identification and lab slip to the receptionist.  there was no one in the waiting room and i chose to stand rather than sit while waiting to be called into the medical laboratory.  the phlebotomist's name was maddie.  i informed her that i had spoken to rihanna, yesterday, who received the new order from my new and current pcp.  maddie was friendly, efficient and professional as she input my contact information and created identification labels for the blood draw tubes.   within a few seconds after applying a rubber strap around my upper arm, maddie located my vein and i barely felt a slight pinch when she inserted that needle.  after she completed the blood draws, she asked me to confirm my contact information on the labels again and then i was done!

i had knee surgery and i was looking for a new and better place to get rehabilitation for my right knee.
kessler rehabilitation center opened up in warren, nj not long ago. i knew they had a good reputation, so i decided to give them a try. i'm so happy i did. 
i called on the phone and i was able to set up several appointments with katie right away. 
my first appointment was with jennifer, and it was more of an evaluation, and just an overall discussion to see what my problems were and what i needed to work on. my second visit and every other visit afterwards was with howard lee. i have been to rehabilitation four times over the years and i have never had a physical therapist as good as howard lee. 
howard took the time to listen to my issues, and address each and everyone of them. howard has a wonderful disposition, and he really had an amazing way of working with each individual patient one on one and customizing each physical therapy session to the patients needs.
howard used different techniques and utilized equipment in different ways that i've never seen or experienced before. howard even noticed my crutches weren't adjusted properly for my height, and readjusted them for me. ( the nurse in the hospital adjusted them before i left.) 
howard even did cupping on me. i won't lie it was very painful, but afterwords it really helped me to feel better and get the swelling down in my leg  faster. howard used athletic tape across my knee and on my thigh and groin area where i was having so much pain do to weakness after my surgery.. it was like night and day when i worked out.  it really helped with the pain and weakness i was experiencing. 
howard is very professional, very knowledgeable, and extremely friendly. on days that i could not push myself, howard would change up my routine completely to work around those issues. i never did the same workout twice except for the recumbent bike to warm up. 
when i went to a previous physical therapy place in town it was like a mass production and over crowding of people. the physical therapist would meet with you for a few minutes and then hand you a chart and you'd be on your own to figure out all the exercises once shown. sometimes i wasn't sure if i was doing it right, but the physical therapist was off to another patient because they would work on four people at once.
my previous surgeon had me stop going because they made my left knee swell so bad, and pushed me way too hard when i wasn't ready. .
kessler never did this! howard lee actually listens and customizes each and every physical therapy workout. 
another good thing was that there were never more than two people in the entire place at the same time. it wasn't a mass produced physical therapy operation like some of the other ones i went to. this was one on one the entire time. kessler was also very thoughtful when i was there, i suffer from severe migraine headaches and they would shut off some of the overhead lights so not to trigger a migraine while i worked out. this could be done because there was only two of us in the entire place along with staff. my knee has come along way, and i even have exercises to do home that howard printed out for me during this coronavirus epidemic. i highly recommend kessler rehabilitation center for anyone young or old who needs to get physical therapy. howard lee even works with cancer patients.

monday, may 4, 2020
"hello, this is cvs caremark calling for tina you have a prescription order ready for a refill.  you can complete this order on the phone."

tuesday, may 5, 2020

i've given birth at this birth center twice. once back in july 2018 and once just a few days ago right in the middle of the covid-19 pandemic. due to the virus, hospitals have no choice but to enforce strict visitation policies. upon hearing the news that we would not be allowed any other visitors this time around, my husband and i were devastated but we understood. i must say that this birth experience was the best one yet, despite it all. it was an incredibly intimate and lovely stay - it was actually so nice not having anyone there and just being able to be with our newborn baby. the nurses did a phenomenal job making us feel at home here. both times i have delivered here, the nurses have been spectacular. i have always felt like a top priority and it genuinely feels like the staff all truly care about their patients. i just can't rave enough about them. they are all wonderful. 

the food is great! my first birth here, i was not as impressed with the food and sent my husband to get take out out in town for most meals. this time, we didn't want him leaving the hospital more than he needed due to covid screenings and just not wanting to be exposed to more people than necessary. i'm glad to say i was happy with almost all of our meals! my husband and i enjoyed them enough to eat all of our breakfasts, lunches and dinners at the hospital for nearly 3.5 days. all of the meals seemed very balanced as well.

as for my actual birth experience, dr. raz was my anesthesiologist who prepped me for my scheduled c-section this time and he was just incredible. so personable and informative...he made getting my spinal block as least traumatic as possible (i absolutely hate needles so it is always very difficult for me enduring them). he made the process fast, made sure i was aware of what was happening and that i was okay throughout the quick process. i will specifically request him to do my spinal if i ever have another baby via c-section here!

of course dr. cobb, the most wonderful obgyn on the planet deserves some praise as well. he is just the absolute best. this time around, i scheduled my c-section with him and at my request, he and the anesthesiologist made sure i could have my drape/sheet lowered just before baby came out so i could see him in his first moments of life. i was also able to hold him on my chest for nearly all of the remainder of the surgery. it was an incredible experience that i will never forget and i just appreciated so much that they allowed me to have as personal of an experience with my c-section as possible. dr. cobb also has a little background in plastic surgery and it shows! my incision looks great, you can barely even tell it's there because it's so low on my bikini line and in a natural fold of my skin. he did a fantastic job. i've had both my kids delivered by dr. cobb and if i have any more children, i will no doubt have him deliver them as well if he is able!

incredible experience top to bottom. i just can't say enough positive things. 

thank you, once again, pomerado and all staff who helped us during our stay for making my birthing experience amazing, even in the middle of a global health pandemic!!!

late friday night (3/20), i experienced shortness of breath and a 100° temperature, along with intermittent coughing, irregular fatigue, and a headache. by saturday morning my temp was down but i did not feel well at all - still had a headache, trouble breathing, fatigue, and was starting to have body aches. i called the office again and requested contact by the on call doctor. it was dr. h again - and he immediately started yelling at me for calling back. he said "what do you want me to do?!" "do you think you have it? then go to the er!" he then got mad at me because he had told me to call if my temp was 100.3° or higher. i told him i had forgotten that part and was concerned as my temp it 100° the night prior, and the shortness of breath i experienced has never happened to me in my life even with asthma. he barely even let me explain myself before continuing to yell at me. i couldn't even get the words out to tell him (he just kept yelling) the remaining symptoms i experienced, and couldn't explain to him this was not a normal asthma symptom of mine. i am 28 years old and have had asthma my entire life - i know what's normal for my body. honestly, i didn't think i had covid-19 and was seeking help for what i was experiencing. also, i told him his tone made me uncomfortable and he continued, so i hung up on him. 

my husband heard this entire interaction as i had the doc on speaker and needless to say - my husband was appalled. i was shaken but my husband suggested letting my actual pcp (dr. delatte) know. so, i then called back and left a voicemail for dr. delatte's assistant. i tried to explain what happened but then started crying in the voicemail (super embarrassing) but i was at a loss. i asked them to contact me when they were back in the office that following monday (3/23) as i no longer wanted to talk to dr. h but am still concerned with how i was feeling, whether or not it's covid-19. it's now april 1st and i have not heard back from dr. delatte or her assistant. over 5 business days is plenty of time to call me back. i don't want a pity call after this review.

i get that we are all stressed during this pandemic, but doctors are the ones we have to rely on if we don't feel well. rather than yell at patients, calmly explain why it's not of concern and offer legitimate support. i've read so many things about this virus and many said people start with the symptoms i had, so god-forbid i was concerned. any doctor that won't allow a patient to even explain their symptoms needs to rethink their profession.

i've been going here for 2-3 years and they have definitely helped in some ways. they diagnosed me with hashimotos when my gp ignored my concerns and made diet and lifestyle recommendations that have helped. 
i have seen other naturopathic practitioners (not at or associated with pmc) and all of them push "their" supplements but i believe that's mainly because that's what they believe will help you/the patient. nds have a more herbal/natural approach to health which mainly includes diet and lifestyle changes vs. modern medications/prescriptions. so if you're looking for a naturopathic doctor than all of them will be very similar in this regard, they will recommend/push supplements (whether it's their own personal brand/blend or an already established company) and diet. that's literally their job, mission, and what their education is based around. i believe the practitioners at pmc are transparent (at least the practitioners i've seen) with supplement/treatment recommendations and that sometimes prescriptions are needed/required. i believe the practitioners are educated, do their best/have the best intentions, and make patients' health a priority. 

where i believe pmc lacks is their business model. i've spent a lot of money out of pocket and been lucky and able to utilize my insurance to help pay for costs. the company charges for things that are sketchy to me. for instance, i think it's ridiculous that they charge a $100 fee to "have your outside labs read". since most normal labs are covered by insurance it's ridiculous to charge patients who choose to use a lab that is covered by their insurance or a cheaper provider. they do testing there that is not normally covered by insurance which is a little more understandable but if their practice made the patient the main priority, they wouldn't charge a ridiculous fee like that. but that's a business practice not the doctors that make that decision. 

i believe they're understaffed which leads to a lot of "administrative" issues, high turnover (which creates misrepresentation and poor and unclear communication among staff and to patients). i've had several staff tell me this throughout my years here. it's nearly impossible to get a hold of anyone on the phone (and don't blame covid-19 because this has occurred since i started there in like 2017). i have been trying to get a copy of a visit invoice for almost 2 months now. when i have gotten someone on the phone they've assured me they were going to send the info to me and i still haven't received it. if you need paperwork like this, a letter of medical necessity, a prescription renewal, etc. make sure you get it before you leave your visit or you may never get it. also, i paid $120 for my last visit and just received an eob from my insurance which stated i should've been charged $108. so that's pretty sketchy. and i can't get a hold of anyone to discuss this... so there's that. 

overall: good clinicians. bad business model.

i figured nothing could phase me after avoiding a nuclear with with iran, dodging an earth-shattering meteor, and now being forced into survival mode by the coronavirus. i needed to get a prescription filled and decided that my local neighborhood mom & pop pharmacy would be the place to go.

i walked into this place with a prescription for something to help with constipation. i was told that they did not have the particular prescription in stock. i gave the pharmacy the physician's contact information to discuss an alternative prescription. after about 15 minutes on the phone, the pharmacy came back and presented me 2 options of a generic drug that they carried, one in powdered form for $45 and one in liquid form for $32. i chose the powdered form since it had a better shelf life.

as it turns out, they sold me the generic version of miralax. for those of you who don't know, miralax is an over-the-counter drug that is available at pretty much any pharmacy (think rite aid, cvs, walgreens). if i had known the alternative to the prescription was miralax, i would have walked 45 seconds down the block to rite aid and bought it for $13.

but no, that didn't happen. here's what happened.

instead of doing the decent thing and telling me to go 45 seconds down the block to rite aid to buy miralax for $13, they sold me the generic stuff for $45. what???

let's just take a moment to let that sink in for a bit. this pharmacy sold me the generic version of an over-the-counter drug for three times the price of what the brand name drug costs. they didn't think for a moment to tell me i could have walked 45 seconds down the block to buy this stuff at a fraction of the price.

that's the kind of pharmacy pyramids rx is. they put money before patients. this will be my first and last time using this pharmacy. i thought humanity would learn to help each other in times of crisis. unfortunately as shown by pyramids rx pharmacy, it was an opportunity to take advantage of a local in need.

long and lengthy but honest review:


results at week 1: 
today marks one week that i got prk eye corrective surgery and i am in the office for my first vision check with dr. law. she is amazing, kind and extremely knowledgeable. i asked her several questions and she was able to give me exact and detailed responses without me feeling rushed in any way. she preformed my eye exams twice. before removing my contacts and again after they were removed. my appointment lasted about 20 minutes and was over before it was even scheduled to start!(since i was early) i learned that my vision is at a (blurry) 20/25 and i was also cleared to drive. that's amazing improvement and i'm very pleased with my results thus far! 

for those worried about getting surgery during a pandemic: (because i was too) 
the office does a great job with cleanliness. there are very few patients in the waiting room at the same time, everyone sits at least one seat apart and they take your temperature as soon as you walk in! they are only allowing patients in the office and any family is asked to wait outside. they offer seating and the downstairs lobby also has a seating area if you wish to wait. (i live very close and always just got dropped off and picked up.) they also have lysol and hand sanitizer everywhere and definitely keep all areas very clean. everyone wears a face mask at all times and all fully cover their mouth and nose. covid-19 doesn't stand a chance! 

about the staff:
i've got to admit, i was very nervous about this surgery and still do not have crystal clear vision but the staff here is just amazing. they are so kind comforting, and welcoming. the doctor that preformed my prk surgery was dr. january and he is just amazing. the staff morale is above par, and it's clear that everyone not only loves their job here but they also love each other! i loved seeing them interact with one another in such a friendly yet professional manner. 

communication with the doctor is super important:
first day i met dr. january he gave me his personal cell phone number & he actually answers very promptly! i sent him texts with questions before surgery and i always got very prompt and detailed replies that made me feel more comfortable and always fully answered my question. after surgery my mom called him on a different phone number, on a sunday morning, and he answered right away. that definitely won over my moms heart and comforted her a lot(and she's never met him).  just goes to say this doctor really cares and is here for all of his patients, and i've never seen this down at such a high level before. there is no lack in communication at this office which is 10/10 in my book. 

about prk:
(i'm not a dr this is my general knowlage) 
prk is different from lasik in that there is no "flap" being made on the cornea. instead, the top layer is painlessly brushed off before being treated by the laser and then they put a prescription-less contact lens in your eye. this is less invasive than lasik but does have a greater and more painful recovery time. (pain only lasts about 2-3 days) there are other pros & cons & i recommend researching it, or asking your doctor about the differences. 

my statistics:
my left eye was at -3.5 and right was at -4.0 with astigmatism. i'm 23 years old, am a masters of accounting student and i am taking an online class through out all of this. (and live & home) 

my personal experience: 
(everyone's eyes are different & your experience could differ from mine!)

day 1 i didn't feel much pain and even managed to finish up a little discussion for school before sleeping the rest of the day. (don't recommend using a computer that early on but i didn't have a choice) my most painful days were days 2(night) till day 4 (morning) & i slept a majority of the day though days 1-4. (if i wasn't sleeping i stayed in a dark room and would ice my eyes & listen to music or funny podcasts) the xanax they gave me honestly didn't work and i had to resort to taking other medications that did give me great relief! the "pain" for me was a constant burning feeling and was more bothersome and annoying than "painful". but once it's gone, it's gone. by day 5-6 i would get headaches from straining to see because of my blurry vision but it's normal and extra strength tylenol helps a lot!! 
i recommend taking 5-7 days off of work/ school for less stress and so you can give your eyes the best ability to heal (my personal opinion) but by day 5 i was already comfortably looking at my zoomed in computer screen. i have not experienced any dry eye issues yet, and am very good at keeping up with my drops.

i was a patient at the integrated wellness bountiful location in 2017 and had nothing but the best experiences.  this one-star review is for the south jordan location.  i went here because it's close to my work, but i will not be returning after this experience.

i sought south jordan's services last week because i was in more pain than i have ever experienced due to a chronic spine issue.  i made it clear to everyone who talked to me that i was in severe pain.  i was visibly immobile.  i am an otherwise healthy 29 year-old woman who couldn't even drive herself to the clinic or open the front door by myself.  that is how much pain my neck and back were in. 

i arrived early for my appointment.  after i signed in, i sat unacknowledged in the lobby for 35 minutes past my appointment time.  when the patient consultation guy finally came to greet me, he said that he could see how stiffly and gingerly i was moving and how painful it looked, which i heartily acknowledged.  

he then had the audacity to ask me to walk around the building on a tour and to ask me right off the bat if committing to a 90 day treatment plan was something i'd agree to.  i said that at that point, i would do anything to feel better and relieve my pain long-term.  i also made sure he knew that i was previously a patient at their bountiful location and that i hoped they'd be able to pull all my records from them so we wouldn't have to start over at square one.   i told him in no uncertain terms that i needed treatment that day for the immense amount of pain i was in.  my neck was visibly swollen and i was having difficulty moving,  breathing and swallowing. i was told that unfortunately, it didn't work that way, and that i would be treated as a brand new patient.  so for the next hour i answered his questions and he took my x-rays.

then he took me to see the nurse practitioner.  jokes were made between them about how i was walking and moving like c-3po (the stiff, robotic droid from star wars, if you're not familiar). i normally have an intact sense of humor, but on this day, when i was in more pain than i've possibly ever been in my life, i did not appreciate the joke. the np took my vitals and mentioned off-handedly an anti-inflammatory cooling rub that i could purchase from them (but that was the last mention of it and i was back at home before i realized i hadn't been given the option to purchase anything) and then i was handed off to the patient consultation guy again.  

he told me how much my visit that day would cost, and i acknowledged i would pay.  he then asked me the most condescending question that a medical professional has ever asked me (ladies, you know what i'm talking about): "is there anyone who is in charge of your financial decisions who should come with you to your next appointment?"

now at this point, i am an hour and a half into this appointment, i'm in excruciating pain, and i've yet to hear a thing about actual treatment or a pain management plan.  as you can imagine, i am almost to my breaking point.  but instead of giving in to the urge to rip off my mask to breathe dragon fire into this man's condescending face, i take a deep breath and say "i am in charge of my own financial decisions.  will the doctor be seeing me soon?"

finally, the chiropractor came in.  he tested my range of movement (very low, no surprises there) and my nerve function, and concluded i had at least two pinched nerves. he then checked his watch, stood up, and said, "alrighty! let's go get you scheduled for your followup exam.  that's when we will discuss your xrays and a treatment plan."

i. was. floored. i told him i was happy to schedule my followup exam, but that i'd come there today for treatment.  i was immobilized from pain and needed something.  an adjustment, a cortisone injection, some massage therapy...anything.  i also hadn't been told what i could do to manage my pain until my next visit.  heat? ice? ibuprofen? should i try to stretch?  why is my neck so swollen? what do my xrays say that i'm paying out of pocket for?

he was a little taken aback, but agreed to do a quick adjustment. he was able to crack my neck, which gave me some temporary relief.  he also told me to ice my neck muscles.  then i scheduled my followup exam--the soonest they could see me is a full week later--and sent me on my way. 

after an ordeal where i was ignored, laughed at, and condescended to for 2 hours, and only given treatment as an afterthought when i insisted upon it, i will not be returning to the south jordan integrated wellness.  i would rather drive 40 minutes out of my way to the bountiful location than ever risk a repetition of the worst patient experience of my life.
