my entire living room ceiling collapsed and since the house was built in the 70's, before i had anyone come in to clean it up, i needed to know if it contained asbestos.

one contractor said they could run the test but it would take 3-4 days and cost $500-600.  what?!  i looked up diy test kits.  those seem to take weeks and are somewhat unreliable.  so i checked for abatement companies and hawaii analytical laboratory popped up in the search.  while not an abatement company, they are a local, accredited lab that does same-day asbestos testing (among many others) for a very reasonable price.

luckily they were open during the pandemic lockdown and were so very helpful.  they explained their prices and what kind of samples to grab.  they also suggested putting up plastic sheeting to minimize any disturbance of the area.

so i donned my asbestos haz mat mask (yes, i actually have one of those), put my samples in ziploc bags and headed to the lab.

the building was unsurprisingly deserted.  i expected a tumbleweed to blow by as the theme from "the good, the bad and the ugly" played in the background.  the woman i spoke to on the phone met me at the door.  she carefully and patiently explained the entire process to me and she helped me consolidate my mess of ziploc bags into nice, cohesive samples.  she explained the options based on how soon i needed the test results.  the 1-2 hour being the most expensive and 4-6 hours being the next.  i opted for the1-2 hour response so i'd still have some fingernails left, plus an abatement contractor was headed over shortly.

and about 1.5 hours later, i got the (unfortunately bad) news.  if i hadn't found them, i would have been waiting for days and paid $600.  instead, i had a nearly immediate result for a very small fraction of the cost.  

and it is a woman-owned company in what i would guess is a male-dominated field.  how cool is that?

so thank you hawaii analytical laboratory!  service above and beyond!

i cannot recommend chemin perez as a midwife because she quit 2 weeks before my due date and 1 week before i gave birth. i received poor communication and concern and realized she was a fear based midwife.
 i will start from the beginning. 
i came to new life midwifery at 3 months. i was taken care of by the assistant midwives, all were very nice. chemin came around rarely. i had a very healthy pregnancy and at 35 weeks my belly measured small. i started to go to the mfm doctor for twice weekly monitoring ( the baby was genetically small on both sides of our family) 
on week 38 i received a call from the mfm doctor telling me that everything was fine and we would continue monitoring for another 2 weeks to decide on a method of delivery. 
an hour later chimen received the same report and called telling me to go to the emergency on call doctor at the hospital to see if they would induce me within the next hour. mind you, this is at the peak of the pandemic where the risks of going to the hospital and especially the emergency doctor are huge. 
i am so lucky that i had my mother with me who is also an obgyn and we were monitoring the baby with her portable ultrasound machine. i had the phone on speaker when chimen was telling me she was transferring me to the care of the doctor on call at the hospital and my mom asked to see the report. after receiving the uploaded report, my mother saw a very normal and healthy baby. it was small (we already knew that) but not disproportionate in any way and with healthy chord and cerebral artery doppler.the mfm doctor had labeled the baby iugr in the 9% and my amniotic fluid levels fluctuating (based on my water intake) chemin had told us that fluid levels shouldn't fluctuate (which is actually very normal) and the chord doppler was at 4.46 when in reality she misread the chord doppler (witch was a healthy 2.18) and mistook it for the cerebral artery doppler. this made her decide not to work with me anymore because she considered me high risk. i felt completely abandoned so close to my due date. i equate it to running a race in first place and your legs giving out right before the finish line, but it this case it was more of the rug being pulled out from under me. 
she also disclosed to us that she had lost a baby last year and she didn't want to take any risks. if i would have known that from the start i wouldn't have gone with her care in the first place. 
i am lucky that i decided to take a 9 week birthing course with kathy killebrew because she ended up saving my pregnancy. chemin had a brief 2 hr video where she explained a few things very shallowly about labor and postpartum. i would have been so ill prepared with what she provided! 
kathy sent us 3 new midwife recommendations and i quickly got to work after having a panic attack.one set of midwives attended my call and it was absolute fate. i was recommended to get a second opinion by dr. fischbein before starting care. he saw the baby as small but symmetrical with a 10/10 ultrasound and good fluid levels at 8.2. 
with a good recommendation nancy beyda and michelle rey were able to attend my delivery!
 i had originally chosen new life midwifery because they take medi-cal, but it doesn't work if she quits. 
we ended up paying for everything out of pocket with the new midwives, but the level of attention and care were so drastically different! 
with chemin, i would update her by text, and the text would be read without a reply. when i asked for recommendations about anything she would say she didn't have any. when i asked about the doctors induction rate that she wanted me to go to she said she didn't think he had one. it was very difficult to get any info.she luckily sent my medical records to the doctor for the second opinion because she did not send them to the new midwives.
at exactly 39 weeks, i had a healthy baby girl weighing 6lbs 6oz from a home water birth without any complications of any kind. if i would have gotten induced early,  my baby would have been born too small and most likely would have had problems.

thank you for taking care such good care of me when i was in so much pain and quite concerend my finger would become infected. it's healing beautifully and i didn't lose my nail.

it's been awhile since i've written a review and since with the covid scare all the restaurants in town are closed i decided to try out one of our longest standing eateries, the powell valley health clinic.  since you can't just leave a single review at such a fine establishment, this is part 1 of 2.  starting off, i would say the curb appeal is better than in the past with multiple extra signs telling you exactly where to park which is helpful when you can't breathe, you're dizzy, and have no depth perception to begin with.  
   you're greeted at the door by what i assume is a welcoming smile behind that mask where you are asked additional questions to further accommodate you.  a hard dry cough, fever, and dizziness even gets you a shiny red sticker on your chest so that others know you've made reservations and you can use the disney-like 'fast pass' line.  a mask, some gloves, and bam! you're in!  
   the maîte d' is of course the first person you'll see, and as the position dictates in any fine establishment, they are very knowledgeable of past stays, have payment info and address on file, and will have any paperwork ready to go to speed up the process.  after just a few quick minutes of waiting...while staring at the assortment of magazines and wondering if i dared touch them...i was called in.  
   at this time i go back and they take measurements, height and weight, and then it's time to see my personal physician's physician's assistant.  some more vitals are taken here and then bam!  one step closer to salvation and feeling better!  next came the physician's assistant - finally! the person i was waiting for.  the physician is gone for the day, but the training everyone here has is impeccable..and if it's not, how would you know? 
     we went through the symptoms again and took a look at my tonsils.  then we called in a physician for a quick consult and take a swab of my tonsils and throat to grow a culture and wham bam, problem solved!  my problem?  i didn't wait long enough to see if it would go away!  silly me!  
     exiting was even easier than coming in with no lines or stops, and since they already knew where to send the bill for my visit i was back in my truck and headed home to try and not die!!  overall my stay left me feeling wanting.  i was in a lot of pain, hadn't been able to swallow since the night before, so no water or food but hopefully it would all work out.  i had no answers, only more questions, and pretty scared to be honest, but i have faith in the people put in place to protect me.  the staff was very pleasant in that small tight-knit country community vibe you've come to expect in powell, and so after saying very painful but socially required thank you's i was out.  
     i feel nothing but the best for this establishment and the people working hard to keep our community safe in these uncertain times.  they're at the front lines - not just when it's in the news, but all the time.  caring for you, your loved ones, and being there for all of us in our most vulnerable moments.  i came back to the powell valley hospital the next day, but as i am not yet done with my current stay i'll have to hold off on writing my next review - spoiler, this will include hotel and restaurant amenities!!

i've struggled (unsuccessfully) with aud (alcohol use disorder) for 30-something years. finally, in 2014 i discovered sinclair method (https://www.the-sinclair-method.com/), which turned out to be a lifesaver. my drinking quickly went down to safe levels and i started to have alcohol free days several times a week. for 5.5 years i was a social drinker, a "normie" in aa speak. 

some life events led to me developing a serious depression and covid lockdown became the last straw. in the beginning of april i stopped taking my medication; from there, my drinking quickly escalated and turned into a heavy 6 weeks binge ending in er, icu and a 10 days detox. after i got back home on may 24, i wanted to make sure that sinclaire is still working (i still had some meds and started taking them right away); i had 3 drinks on the first day, then it went 1, 1, 0, 1, 0 - amazing, considering my condition before the detox. 

by then, i found an outpatient program (iop) at good sam behavioral. i was surprised to learn that dr cecil a. bradley, who prescribed me naltrexone all these years, is the medical director of this program. the program seemed very useful since a) it is in person, no zoom, b) i could address my underlying emotional issues and c) i could get an extended medical leave, since i was not ready to get back to work yet. on thursday, may 28 i was admitted; i was very open about what i've been doing before, what brought me there and about my intentions (go back on sinclaire, since it works great and aa stopped working for me at some point). everybody seemed to be open-minded, accepting and approving of my course of treatment. some even wrote down the name of my method and said they were curious and want to learn more about it. 

on friday noon dr bradley showed up, took me to his office and told me that their program is based on full abstinence and if i kept up the controlled drinking, i'd have to leave. he said there are alternatives to aa and suggested some other program - he just could remember it's name. he is in his 80s and seems to forget things. i promised to think about it over the weekend and tell him about my decision on monday. after all, at this point i could possibly refrain from drinking for the duration of the program.

however, on monday my case manager handed me a recovery plan with mandatory conditions: attend at least 3 meetings a week, find a sponsor and report progress at each morning session. i told her i don't do aa, and i was told to go talk to dr bradley, and again he gave me a dilemma: full abstinence and meetings or leave the program. "if you don't want aa, there is this other program - can't remember it's name... rational recovery?" "- smart recovery?" "- yes, this must be it". "- how is it better than aa?". "- i don't know. we require full abstinence and meetings". so i informed him that i'm quitting and went home.

this got me thinking: 1) why did dr bradley prescribe naltrexone all these years and even wrote me another 3 refills on that monday if he disapproves on sinclair method so much? 2) how does a doctor send a patient to some program can't even remember the name of? did he do any research or he really doesn't care? 3) why did they admit me at all, knowing full well my intentions and dr bradley's position and giving me false hope? 4) what kind of doctors put a patient into completely unscientific, faith-based programs with abysmal success rates and force him to abandon something that is proven to work for 80% and this patient in particular?

so i googled dr bradley and discovered that the medical board of california twice has suspended his license, once in 1990 and second time in 2007 (http://www.psychcrime.org/news/index.php?vd=32&t=california+disciplines+psychiatrist+cecil+bradley) he also was known to be sending referrals to life choices and working at red road recovery, two rehabs run by the same person, richard franko, who has no certifications and is a drug addict himself. life choices were reported to california's dhcs for "making parolees assist in human like slave duties as a condition of not sending these clients back to prison. dhcs investigators heard from people they interviewed that franko had indeed used clients for personal benefit and, in doing so, compromised their sobriety." (https://www.sanjoseinside.com/news/rehab-owners-who-lost-license-amid-shocking-allegations-deny-charges-get-back-to-business/)

makes you wonder, how does a doctor like cecil bradley ends up a medical director in well-respected hospital like good sam? i would not recommend going to good sam in- or outpatient behavioral programs until they replace him. the rest of the staff seems to be great, but there is nothing they could do to help me under current leadership.

i recently had prk done, and i have nothing but great things to say about diamond vision. i initially signed up for a consultation in march, right before everything started closing due to the pandemic. however, the clinic closed before i was able to come in. despite this, ken was able to provide a consultation over the phone for me, where he explained everything about the procedure and told me things i didn't even think to ask to make sure that i had all the information i needed to make an informed decision. he was extremely friendly, and i really appreciated that he took 45 minutes on a call to ensure that i had all my questions answered. i was concerned that my high astigmatism could be an issue, but it was well within the treatment limits. i had -4.25 in my left eye, -3.75 in my right, and -2.75 diopters of astigmatism in both eyes.

the office was closed for about 2 months where during that time, sofia kept me updated by calling me every few weeks to let me know the current situation and when they expected to reopen. i appreciated that she took the time to do this, whereas some of the other clinics where i signed up for consultations had completely neglected to do so after the first consultation. this fact that the staff at diamond vision didn't keep me in the dark really showed me that they actually cared about me as a patient.

my pre-op exam took no more than 1.5 hours and required a $200 refundable deposit that goes towards the cost of the surgery to compensate for the doctor's time. ken met me that day to perform some tests on my eyes such as measuring the topography of my cornea and the strength/pressure of my cornea using the air puff test. not every clinic performs the air puff test, so i knew that they were conducting a comprehensive exam to ensure that i was a good candidate. ken also told me that my dilated pupil size is within the treatment zone, which is very important information to know because this will directly affect your night vision.

after this, i was told that due to my corneal thickness, i would have to get prk instead of lasik. i was leaning more towards prk anyway because it is the more conservative approach and i wanted a lower risk of complications in the future, so i had already done my research on the procedure. regardless, dr. stein went over the entire procedure and made sure that i had all my questions answered. i was prescribed steroid, antibiotic, and nsaid eyedrops, ibuprofen, and a pill to take before the procedure to help calm down.

on the day of the procedure, i was in the office for 2 hours. after filling out the paperwork which basically acknowledges that you understand the risks and consent to the procedure, dr. stetson, the surgeon, went over some details with me. he advised me to avoid uv exposure so that my eyes don't heal too aggressively. it's important to wear sunglasses when going outside during the time your eyes are healing so that the sun doesn't adversely affect them. the actual procedure was very quick and painless. i noticed that dr. stetson used an amoils scrubber (a brush) to remove the epithelium, which minimizes healing time compared to a blunt scrape, which other surgeons use. the actual procedure probably took less than 15 minutes for both eyes and i could immediately notice the difference. i was made aware that my vision will get worse through days 3-5 post-op and that i will notice some fuzziness due to the bandage contact lens placed on my eyes. this will be removed at my 1-week post-op.

throughout this whole experience, i was very impressed by how they handled the reopening of the office during the pandemic by limiting the number of appointments in any given day to minimize the number of people in the waiting room, as well as asking family members to remain outside of the office as to not congregate together. the office was kept very light to minimize human-to-human contact. everyone was wearing masks and the staff was meticulously disinfecting every surface that we touch and the machines that were used to conduct the tests. i felt extremely safe and was happy to see how seriously they were taking this situation. this is another way that the staff showed that they really care about the health and safety of their patients.

some important things to note is that if you are doing prk, your vision may take up to 3 months to stabilize, so the healing process is pretty slow. additionally, if you purchase the lifetime warranty, you must attend all your follow-up appointments and get your vision checked annually, either at diamond vision or another clinic of your choice.

overall, i am very happy that out of the 5 clinics i was comparing, i chose diamond vision. i am very impressed by how friendly the staff was (ken and sofia especially!), in addition to dr. stetson's expertise and prior background in operating on military pilots. i highly recommend diamond vision and can confidently say you will not be disappointed!

i went to rma because i had heard their name floated by people in the lgbtq community i knew had used reproductive technology. i called and they had immediate availability and friendly staff up front who were able to tell me on the phone that an iui cycle cost $1200 without insurance coverage, so we went into a consult ($150 without insurance coverage, half off because they were running via videochat due to covid-19). from there on, the experience was really not good, and made me feel pretty crappy, although due to timing and initial investment issues, we did proceed with them for a cycle. i wish that i had listened to the earlier review on this page stating that this practice is not lgbtq friendly. long review below, but essentially i would advise going to a queer friendly midwifery practice and/or perhaps main line fertility as mentioned in the other review.

this practice and its procedures are all designed for cis hetero people who have been trying to conceive through sex and are dealing with infertility. it's just clear every step of the way that it's not designed for you, and i might have been okay with that but the lack of empathy around some of the barriers particular to queer people trying to conceive was just kind of painful. a little sympathy and acknowledgement that this system was not designed for us - for example, the thousands of dollars they would charge to use a known sperm donor (close friend whom we trust) due to needing to subject him to fda screening that would not be required of a sexually intimate i.e. hetero partner, refusing to use fresh donor sperm for iui due to same requirements to "protect you" (except it doesn't feel protective, it feels oppressive) - and interest in accommodating our particular situation would have gone a long way. [sidenote: i dunno if it's legally different or whatever, but midwives do not put you through this bs and can do fresh sperm known donor iui for a couple hundred $]. i actually work in healthcare and thought i knew what i was getting into, but pregnancy stuff leaves you feeling surprisingly vulnerable, and i was surprised at how helpless and unheard i felt at rma and how upsetting that was.

something i didn't know when i did the $150 consult is that other practices (including the philadelphia midwife collective and main line fertility) will work with you to have this covered by insurance even if your insurance doesn't cover fertility treatments at all. they can bill it as a women's health visit for well woman, infertility, stuff like that. 

rma is a big practice despite the deceptively small number of physicians and it runs kind of like an assembly line. the care kind of felt like there was a fast-moving train and you needed to either get on it, get run over, or get left behind. they knew how to do what they usually do and weren't about to get creative for you. communication is difficult in that you communicate via messaging on a patient portal with nurse practitioners. i think they are answering a lot of email because they are kind of brusque at times, though i don't think they meant it badly. to talk to your team, you call a central processing center, and then they have to call the nursing staff for you, who then call you back. this led to things like panicking for several days about a lab result that it turned out didn't really mean anything significant but was initially made to sound like we should delay a month (we have a limited window to conceive for various personal reasons) or have added risks in pregnancy. you really don't get much time with the doctors who are perhaps more knowledgeable and flexible in what they can offer. 

what they offer is high intervention infertility treatments - they will suggest you do all the things at significant expense, from fallopian tube studies to genetic testing, even if there is no reason to believe you have any biological infertility. at times, i felt somewhat bullied/guilted/manipulated into doing some of these expensive things even when they were stated to be optional, as though i were cutting corners or being a bad mom, and i was made to feel like i was being annoying by keeping asking what was absolutely required vs optional and how much things cost. in the consult, they said a financial counselor would call a day after, but it really took 2 weeks and multiple calls from me. then as soon as something changed last minute in clinic, since the clinic front desk staff weren't financial counselors and there was a whirlwind of blood draws and then by the time i got to ask the doctor about it she already had a very expensive ultrasound probe up my vagina, i ended up undergoing this ultrasound/labs for $700 or so. had i known it wasn't going to be included in my iui package if i had to delay insemination until the next month, i would have tried to opt out. but that's the kind of flexibility they really just aren't very set up for - maybe most of their patients have insurance and aren't worried about it.

as of april 2, california had a relatively low number of coronavirus cases per capita, compared to new york, new jersey, and louisiana.  california health officials and politicians, don't pat yourself on the back just yet.  just check the number of covid-19 tests processed: new york 239,000 and california 33,000.  

as of march 31, one of california's major commercial lab testers of covid-19, quest diagnostics, had 115,000 covid-19 test results pending in 12 labs across the country.   this is due partly to a shortage of trained technicians to run the lab test machines, and a shortage of the testing reagents, many of which imported from china and other countries.  california itself has 59,500 covid-19 test results pending, with test results taking up to 10 days.  the state with the second most reported pending results is florida with 77,000 tests processed and 1,280 covid-19 test results pending. 

trump got his second covid-19 test result in 15 minutes.  much more essential people like emergency room doctors, er nurses, critical care nurses, anesthesiologists, nurse anesthetists, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, respiratory therapists, respiratory therapist technicians, intensive care technicians, emergency medical technicians, medical workers, health care workers, paramedics, medical first responders, police, and firefighters have been quarantined at home, away from work, for 10-12 days before finding out their covid-19 result were negative!  

worse yet, such an essential worker, negative at the time of testing, could be infected within the 10 day test result waiting period, receive their negative result from 10 days earlier, show no symptoms, and then go back to work infecting their professional work colleagues in addition to the patients they contact.

patient stays longer in hospitals awaiting covid-19 test results of up to 10 days.  subsequent heavier demands and usage of hospital staffing, hospital supplies, hospital bedding availability, and personal protective equipment, all of which already in short supply.    

an out patient may have flown on a full airplane, ridden on a bus, or gone to overcrowded stores like costco or walmart, infecting countless others, by the time a positive result is obtained 10 days later.     

the state is looking for other private labs to run covid-19 tests.  abbott labs just rolled out a covid-19 test that can get results in 5-13 minutes, manufacturing up to 50,000 test cartridges a day.  the white house gets them, but gives each state only 15 machines and 100 cartridges of these test kits.  so wyoming with 579,000 people gets the same number of test kits as california with 39,900,000 people.  we will have to continue to rely on getting results from quest diagnostics, with results taking  up to 10 days.  

california's april 3 count of 11290 coronavirus cases may be that of 10 days earlier-march 24, and is completely misleading.  the actual number of positive covid-19 results as of april 3 may be triple that, but won't be reported until 10 days from now, on april 13.

on the positive side: quest diagnostics backlog of 115,000 pending covid-19 test results on march 31 is an improvement of the 160,000 pending covid-19 test results on march 25.

april 21 update: new york has processed 669,982 tests or 34,151 per million residents, ranking 1st of the 50 states.  california has processed 300,100 tests or 7,666 per million residents, ranking 46th of the 50 states. 

on april 19 a panel of experts published a report saying that to begin to open up the country, 5 million tests would have to be processed daily.  to bring the economy up to full speed, 30 million tests would have to be processed daily.  not going to happen relying on private labs like quest diagnostics.

i truly believe dr. lisa abaid saved my life. i had been experiencing sharp, odd pelvic pains for quite some time, but my previous obgyn always minimized it/me, often making me feel ignorant. 
i requested an ultrasound so many times during annual check ups, but she always mocked me with a scoff.  she literally stated, "theres no reason for an ultrasound.... nobody's going to approve a hysterectomy in your case," with one foot already out the door, but that's a totally different review....

everyone was so worried that i had ovarian cancer, so i kept pushing my requests. later, my ultrasound revealed everything from uterine fibroids to complex masses of cysts that had overtaken all my female organs. 

in normal cases, small cysts come and go, but mine found their way inside my ovaries since they were undetected for years. the only way i can explain it is that over time, everything started attaching together like a bunch of grapes, morphing into one complex mass.  

after viewing my ultrasound and doing a pelvic exam on me, dr. abaid knew exactly what was wrong. she explained all the scenarios from a conservative perspective to a more proactive approach.  i trusted her recommendation for a laparoscopy and surgery. 

in the midst of our current pandemic, it should've been a 2-3 week wait to get scheduled for surgery, but dr. abaid was able to get me in within one week. i truly believe that if we had waited any longer, it would've definitely tuned into cancer.  i believe we caught it just in time. 

it's no wonder why everyone from the rns to the anesthesiologist told me that she's like "the gold standard" in her field. "someone must be looking out for you," is what one nurse literally told me....

this was exactly the assurance i needed at that precise moment of all the chaos going on. what's more is that instead of making a long, vertical caesarian incision, she was able to make a few tiny incisions that will eventually look like tiny marks.  (sorry if the photos are tmi, but her work is so amazing that i just had to share this with women in oc)

god bless dr. lisa abaid.

here are three tips, from going through two pregnancies here:
-yes, they run late. i've had everything from 5-10 minutes to almost two hours late. it seems to be at a higher frequency than other medical offices. the early morning appointments seem to be better than later in the day; if time is a concern, try to get in early. otherwise, be ready to wait.
that said: if they're running super late, it is likely because someone - another patient - is having a very bad day with pregnancy complications or pregnancy loss. try to remember that and don't take it out on the staff!
-yes, their practitioners are often in and out of the room quickly due to the high volume of patients. 
the takeaway: if the docs/techs are in and out pretty quickly, it means that you're normal and healthy. take it as a positive thing.
-and a small warning: the genetic counselors are a separate office, even if they call themselves part of the larger facility. check with your insurance before booking with them to see about coverage. we got a "surprise" bill 5 months later that our insurance denied coverage for as they were not in-network. 
also, don't complain about their covid-19 rules. does it suck that my partner can't come to these appointments? yes. is there a single thing the office can do about it? nope. with their high-risk patients, they're doing exactly what needs to be done to protect vulnerable people.

(not what i was quoted on the phone at 6:00 a.m.)
 i was surprised that the nurse asked me for sanitizer hand wipes, during her visit, because she had none with her. apparently, they were out. 
the lack of any professionalism is starting to scare me as i look back on it. 
the results came back negative for influenza and strep.
then the doctor came thru on skpe to ask me more questions to see if i qualified again for the covid19 test.  the nurse swabbed my nose again, for the covid19 test, now as my appointment was winding down, i was advised that the for results of the test there was an additional charge of another $50.00. i actually said no more money! he could email me or i will call for results. the nurse said she didn't know how that would work out, but understood, and would relay the message to the doctor. 
honestly. i feel this is deceptive trade practices along with profiteering from the corona virus. i'm upset that my p.c.p. would send me to someone who did not take any insurance. people are desperate right now and confused like myself over this process. who can afford to pay over $600 for a test, people have to be tested but should not be taken advantage of. i'm now thinking that i may have not gotten a valid test because of these deceptive trade practices. the result are supposed to be available in 36 hours from 08:00hrs this morning 3-19-2020. not sure i will be getting result since i did not pay the $50.00.  i will be calling and looking on line for my results. i'm sure the federal government who said these tests are free will be very shocked when they get this bill.  and i did find out from my insurance company they won't pay that provider. 

i appreciate your taking time to read this, i feel these tactics of not telling a person up front what the true charge are is probably illegal.  the fact that they are not recognized by any insurance company too is troubling.

tldr; if you have a baby that isn't sleeping 12 hours a night, call vivian now. hiring her, was one of the best investments we've made and she helped our 5mo old baby sleep through the night and get on a consistent schedule in less than a week. 

long version: when i first had my baby, i had subscribed, like many, to taking cara babies online. why hire a sleep trainer when i had resources like this at my fingertips? by 5 months, we thought things were relatively good from a sleep perspective - baby was napping ~4-5 times per day and only waking 1-2 times per night. i figured it couldn't get much better until one of my good friends hired vivian and within 2 nights had a baby who was on 3 consistent naps per day and sleeping 12+ hours a night. i called vivian immediately.

on the initial call, she asked me a lot of questions about babies age, weight, current sleep habits, etc and at the end said she could get her on longer, fewer naps in the day and sleeping through the night in 3-5 nights. and she was right. on night one, we pulled all the sleep "crutches"...no more merlin, no pacifier, no dream feed. by night 2, baby was falling asleep in less than half the time it used to take with the pacifier and sleeping in longer stretches. by night 3, baby was going down for naps in under 3 minutes with zero crying and on a daytime sleep schedule that was much more predictable, giving both my husband and i the ability to plan our days better and leave the "waiting for baby to wake up limbo". it's now been one full week since starting and we've had 3 nights of 12 hours sleep, her average time to fall asleep is 2-4 minutes after putting her down in her crib, and she's a happier baby for it. 

vivian knows her stuff. you have to follow her rules exactly, and they may seem harsh or different from what you were doing before, but they work and they work fast. she was so supportive during the entire process and held us super accountable, calling us first thing every morning and multiple times a day to check on how her naps went. for me, that was the biggest difference between hiring vivian vs using an online teaching tool like taking cara...her constant check ins and availability to call on the spot and ask questions.

bonus - we hired her during this crazy covid-19 shut down. rather than come in house, she provided us unlimited phone support which i actually preferred. i've enjoyed getting to know vivian on a personal level as well and couldn't recommend her highly enough. my only regret was not calling her sooner!

i have donated blood here many times in the past. i did not donate for awhile due to a busy schedule and low hemoglobin levels, but things have calmed down and i take iron supplements now so hopefully i can donate more frequently. 
today the process was a bit different than before due to covid-19 protocols. i made an appointment online which was quick and easy. i was able to fill out the health questionnaire online which was also easy, and then print out a ticket to bring with me for the donation. this saved about ten minutes at the donation center.
they take your temperature with a forehead scanning device before you check-in. masks are required to be worn by donors and staff. they also do a good job at keeping donors six feet away from each other. check-in was smooth and the staff member was nice. theresa took my vitals and was very friendly. a few more questions and it was time to donate.
i donated double red blood cells. a slightly higher hemoglobin level is required for this type of donation. basically they remove the red blood cells and return other blood components back to you in a saline solution. i usually feel better after this type of donation! sometimes you can get cold, but they have heat packs (or blankets before covid-19). you can also feel a tingling sensation during the return of the other blood components, but it passes quickly. this donation takes about 30 minutes (whole blood donation takes about 10-15 minutes). mike was in charge of my donation. he was great...painless insertion of the needle, hit the vein in the first try, checked on me frequently, and explained the whole process. the staff here are very nice and appreciative of your donation.
before, during, and after the donation they offer you water and snacks (sweet or salty). they also check on you frequently to be sure you feel ok and are not having any discomfort.
they do not rush you out of the donor chair and recommend waiting in the building for 15 minutes to be sure you do not have a reaction to donating. they give you a sheet at checkout with your blood pressure, blood type, and hemoglobin level. you can also go online to get your vitals and cholesterol levels too. 
they walked me to the front of the building after my donation since they are using overflow rooms in the back to keep social distancing in place. the building is clean, and a very pleasant environment. they have plenty of flat screen tvs to watch while waiting and donating (not in the overflow rooms however).  i highly recommend donating blood here whether you are a first time donor or have donated before.

cough
shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
fever
chills
muscle pain
sore throat
new loss of taste or smell
other less common symptoms have been reported, including gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
trouble breathing
persistent pain or pressure in the chest
new confusion
inability to wake or stay awake
bluish lips or face

all in all, it just baffles me that a medical clinic would turn away someone who has potentially severe medical issues. nowhere on this list is my symptom of lower abdominal pain.

grocery pickup: aweful!

let's start with the ordering. i hope you don't really need anything you order. because if they don't have it in stock, you won't know until you get there. and no substitutions. for example; you want 2% milk? cool. pick  your brand. if they are out of that brand, you are not getting milk, even if they have it in another brand.
how about meat? you'd better be a really good guesser. meat is ordered by weight,  not package. you want a pound of burger? well, if the packages are a pound and an ounce you aren't getting it. how about a whole chicken? you'd better know exactly what one weighs, and they better have that exact weight ready to go, or no chicken!
ok, you've gambled your weekly budget on food you may or may not actually receive, now let's pick your appointment time! have a leisurely wait in your car while they figure out where your stuff is. bring a book.
i arrived right at 4:30 for my 4:30 pickup. i called 3 times to let them know i was here before anyone answered. i then waited an additional 20 minutes before my things were brought out. 
one silver lining, the person that brought the bags was very friendly and pleasant.
upon arriving home and unpacking my groceries, i noticed some items missing. my receipt showed just as many "not available" as checked off items. no meat, no dairy, nothing cold, and most of my veggies were not there. many of the checked off items were not in my order.
i contacted customer service, and left a message. then, i headed out to my other local store to complete my grocery shopping.
the following week i receive a call from weis! guess what? my cold items were found! sitting in the back of some cooler, and starting to spoil. would i be down to get them? no, i don't think so.
when i asked for a refund of the items, the associate explained that she had no idea how to do that. i could have a gift card for store credit? or maybe cash?
i asked to be called back when she figures out how to refund me. we'll see if that happens...
all in all i am not a happy customer. there are gaping holes in this system and obvious lacking communication. i get that we are all facing a challenge to the normal way of things. each of us needs to be patient and understanding. but, wow.

update: while typing this i received a call from customer service. they are processing my refund and just as stressed as i am about the whole process. we're all in this together.

 no!).  despite getting an email broadcasting that they were offering telehealth appointments during the pandemic (which prompted me to call), she then went on about not being sure how it would be charged because it was telehealth (not in-person standard office visit) and she "didn't have any codes for a telehealth visit."  i asked who would have the code so we could find out the cost, she said the "billing person" who wouldn't be back in the office for several days. i then asked to speak with the office manager and asked why they were email blasting advertising for telehealth appointments yet unable to tell me what i would be charged. he also tried to obfuscate with all kinds of gibberish and basically said that they won't know until after the appointment whether they would want to bill it as a 'level 3' or 'level 4' (gee, that clears it right up for me given i know what that jargon means for pricing implications).  even after i explained that i simply needed the dr. to look over the allergy blood test results that my son's gi dr. ordered to see if there were specific foods he was reacting to that might be triggering his inflammation, he refused to tell me if that would require 'level 3' or 'level 4' service.  basically, they wanted me to make an appointment, come in, and let them charge my insurance whatever they wanted afterward. i said no thanks  i'll move on to a dr. who is more transparent and straightforward with their costs.  thanks for wasting 25 minutes of time for nothing. in what alternate reality do the people running this practice live in that they think they don't need to tell customers the upfront pricing of their services?  would i take a pile of dry cleaning in and say, "here you go, just clean this and let me know afterward what your prices are, thank you."? no!  would i hire a builder, give them my plans, and then say, "build my house and just let me know when you're all done what that cost will be?"  the arrogance and duplicity of this office was astounding.

my wife and i chose dr. tiffany chen after extensive research. we loved her relaxing calm demeanor and her confidence. i have taken a little while to write this review as it's been a crazy month with covid taking its toll on the country. my wife and i are 45, and this was our 5th and final attempt to have a baby with ivf. dr. chen was very aware of how invested we were and took very good care of us all the way through. we decided to induce a week early on 3-8-2020. we went in on 3-7 to start the ripening of the cervix. by 10 pm on 3-8 everything was starting to move and my wife got her epidural. dr. chen was on a 24 hour shift and was scheduled to leave at 7 am. we knew this and were getting anxious to have our baby and have dr. chen deliver her.  at 7 dr. chen came in and said she wanted to stay a little longer after her shift because she was so invested with us and our baby. by 9 am things were starting to move. at 9:40 our daughter got caught in the birth canal. shoulder dystocia happens when the baby's shoulder gets caught behind the mother's pubic bone. within seconds dr. chen went into action, she declared it an emergency and at least a dozen people started running into our room. i was pushed aside and five people started working on getting our baby out as quickly as possible as she was being starved of oxygen. as brief background, my sister's son had the same birth issue, but was caught in the birth canal too long. he spent 36 days at children's hospital after a life flight from yakima. he almost died a couple times and we were told he would be mentally handicapped for life, etc. he turned out fine, but we were very aware of what can happen with shoulder dystocia.
 
during this entire ordeal dr. chen stayed calm, while i did not, and she had our daughter out in less than a minute and a half. she immediately handed her to the emergency personnel that had ran into help and it took them a 1:45 to get her to start breathing. she had the breathing mask on and everything. the second she made her first cry our hearts started beating again. she was pulled out and resuscitated so quickly that she had zero issues despite her traumatic birth. we came to find out that dr. chen's office practices this technique weekly to prepare for this kind of emergency. we feel as though we owe our daughter's health to dr. chen. had she not stayed almost four hours after her shift and had she not practiced this emergency procedure to the extent that she had, we feel that we would have been in the same predicament that my sister went through with an extended hospital stay and fighting to keep our baby alive. if you read this dr. chen, we are forever grateful for you and your attention to us. our daughter is wonderful and we owe a lot of that to you. thank you from the fullness of our hearts.

i understand the quarantine has affected everyone, but especially those in healthcare. i am a registered nurse working in acute care in the hospital. i am very much affected by covid. if i had known that my appointment was cancelled, i would have gone in to work that day. since i received that mass e-mail stating that new look skin center will be open as usual, i decided to keep my appointment instead of having to go through the hassle of rescheduling. when in the end, it was more of a hassle and waste of time driving all the way to new look skin center that day, and finding locked doors is how i came to learn my appointment was cancelled. it is extremely inconvenient and stressful not just as a customer, but as a healthcare worker on the front line, to not be notified of a cancelled appointment. again, i could have gone into work that day, but as i previously stated, i scheduled around this appointment with new look skin center. if a courtesy e-mail was made stating that the business would remain open, then another courtesy e-mail could have easily been made from new look skin center stating that they will be closed. people make appointments with the idea that their appointments will happen. it is negligent to have sent a first mass e-mail stating new look skin center will be open without sending another mass e-mail that the business will be closed to make clients aware of the closure. both as a customer and as a healthcare worker on the front line, it is very inconsiderate and a waste of time to have driven all the way to new look skin center & not have been notified of the business' closure.

- i'm not sure where to share my frustration but decided to start here.

having had a severe sore throat, cough and congestion for about a week, i went to my doctor (wearing a mask they gave me) yesterday.  i was told that i likely just had a severe sinus infection (non-contagious) but that i should probably consider being tested for covid 19.  they suggested that i go to the drive through testing at baptist east; so i did.

there was a quick drive through triage with two stops to determine that i "qualified" for testing.  then they instructed me to park my car, where i was called on my phone and told it was my turn for testing.  this all took no more than 10 minutes.  when i arrived at the first of two stops at the testing tent, i was asked for my insurance card and asked how much i wanted to put toward my $1400 deductible.  when i asked what the cost would be for the test, they told me that they did not know but that i would need to pay "something" toward my deductible for the emergency department visit.  emergency department visit!  you have to be kidding me!   those visits cost hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars and i was in a rickety tent in a parking lot trying to do my part to determine if i had exposed anyone to a terrible virus.   i got nowhere when asked why this was considered an emergency department visit instead of a minor medical or minute clinic visit.  i also told the payment staff that they should disclose the approximate cost at the very beginning of the testing process.  nonetheless, i put $50 on my credit card and proceeded to the second section of the tent to be tested for the common good.

two nurses swarmed me as i sat down in the testing section of the tent.  one took vitals while the other gave me a new set of sinus windows with five different swabs.  when i asked why so many, i was informed that they are testing for the flu, strep, covid 19 and one or two other tests.  five tests in all.  i told her that i had no idea they were going to do all those tests but she said that's what they are testing for at the current time.  and i am sure they are profiting for each and every separate test for each and every person being tested.  i went back to my car, a bit stunned from the encounter, and comforted my bleeding nostril with a tissue.

the covid-19 testing at baptist east took less that being in line at chic-fil-a and should definitely not be billed as an emergency department visit.  i feel that the hospital is taking advantage of the pandemic instead of doing its share to help those affected.  they should know better.  and they should be ashamed.

marian regional medical center had the best newborn baby and mommy care i could have ever imagined.  their doctors and nurses were knowledgeable, extremely attentive, and caring.  we were proud to have had both of our sons in this facility.  the experience could not have been better.

and then there is the emergency room.  our visits with our sick kids were anything but a pleasant experience.  they amounted to nothing more than:

"hey, your son has a fever and an ear infection, but sometimes fevers are a good thing, so just let it ride.  here's a bill for $500-700".  "he'll be able to sleep once he's exhausted from the pain."  we learned to rely on our physician for much better care solely.

today, i received a frantic call from my wife stating that her mom fell down the stairs, and she called the ambulance.  the ambulance brought her to marian.  when i got to marian, the nurses were dismissive.  i told them who i was and asked if my wife was with her mom.  her mother has dementia and can't always speak for herself.  i don't know what was done with my mother-in-law because the nurses wouldn't even entertain my questions.  the nurse there gave me a number to call but then told not to call because the nurses would be busy.  what the heck kind of response is that?  they wouldn't even tell me if she was breathing.

my wife provided them with legal and medical documents stating that fact.  the staff didn't review the documents my wife submitted adequately.  her mom's hospital paperwork contained nothing regarding a living will or legal responsibility.  the staff didn't give her the time of day.  additionally, due to covid-19 precautions, my wife still was not allowed to be by her side.  these actions appear to be contrary to the dignity health website.  

we called around the hospital directory and reached the floor manager who, unlike those greeting patients, was very understandable.  she put us through to the nurse treating my wife's mom.  the nurse exhibited professionalism on the phone and thankfully allowed us to speak with her mom.  her mom was very curt regarding how they handled her.  

the nurse ultimately notified us that they performed all necessary checks, and there were no fractures of any kind.  when we inquired about the possibility of a fracture she sustained in her spine, before this event, becoming worse as a result of the fall, suddenly, they spotted the fracture.  they would not pursue an mri to determine if the fracture became worse.  

in the end, they said, "good-to-go," gave her some pill and left her behind the doors to the emergency room lobby waiting for me to show up, alone, with her belongings inside of a trash bag.  my mother-in-law was so angry.  it's like they handled her akin to something in a production line.  

marian should not pretend to be filled with blindly compliant staff.  if it happened to any of their loved ones, you know they would be there as an advocate or as a visitor.  my wife wasn't a visitor wanting to spend time with mommy.  she was to speak for her legally and medically.  it would have saved time for everyone involved.  in this manner, people wouldn't have rushed to read the results of the examination and get it wrong.    

it's a tough job the er staff chose--no doubt about it.  however, it's human beings and their advocates you're handling.

i got to spend two nights here recently. luckily i wasn't the patient -- but i kept my man company after his surgery. i actually slept on two chairs bedside while he was there. 

i've been here before myself, but they seem to have upped their game. in addition to taking all the extra precautions for covid, every person we came in contact with was very professional and enjoyable to deal with -- from the cleaners on up to the doctors and nurses. there really was a great team effort. and it shows.

the food here was surprisingly way better than average for hospital food. every morning starting at 6:30 am you can call in your breakfast order from their menu. it takes about an hour or less to get your hot breakfast. you use your phone to call the kitchen extension. (hint: they're busy. don't hang up. just hold til they answer.) choices included various omelets, eggs, turkey sausage, potatoes, breads/cakes, fresh and canned fruits, juices, cereals, etc. the only thing they didn't have was toast! you also call in for your other meals at least an hour or so in advance. lunches, too, were good as well as dinners. there's a lot of variety and they try to accommodate all requests if possible. two standouts were their fresh sliced hot turkey with mashed potatoes and gravy and their mac n cheese.

the hospital offers free valet parking which is helpful as the lot fills up. 

the only downside was the day we came their computers were acting up so it  took longer to register and to be processed during pre-op. and a longer time than expected waiting for a room to be available. 

no one really wants to be in a hospital, but if you do need to be, this is one of the better options in town.

ok so here's my review. i have had some bad allergies for the past couple months. i noticed back in november and december how bad it was and the. it went away. then in early march being sent home to work from home due to covid they kicked back in. my guess was i was allergic to my cats. i've had them for 5 years and suddenly i'm getting the sore throat feeling and redness and a dry mouth feeling.

come the day of the skin test. i had an appointment at 1215. i was literally 2min late. i got a phone call at exactly 1215 asking where i was. i came in and apologized and was told at the front desk "if you aren't 15min early to check in you are considered late". so this time around i thought it was strange because they didn't even check my vitals. the positive about the skin test was yes i did find out i was allergic to my cats as well as some other things too.

fast fwd to this week. still having a scratchy feeling in my throat. yesterday i called twice. was told "she's off today we will contact you tmr on a medication she suggests". come today i call 2 more times and get voice mails. not even a call back. so i decide to go to walgreens and talk to my pharmacist. she had told me that yes the dry mouth i have been having is part of the reaction to my cats and suggested a tablet that dissolves in my mouth. looked up my chart and told me "yes these are all just over the counter medications". she then suggested i try claritin for the time being. i let the pharmacist know i scheduled a new appointment with a new allergist with an actual dr and not a pa. the pharmacist also told me how there are a bunch of prescriptions and different kind of steroids as well that can be taken to help reduce symptoms.

i wish this store would do a little more education on social distancing and proper use of masks as their employees repeated take unnecessary risks with their own health and the health of customers, many of whom are picking up meds for comorbidities that put them at increased risk of  severe covid19 infections.

masks don't protect your customers or coworkers when worn on your chin or around your neck. masks need to cover both your nose and mouth. masks are not a substitute for social distancing. surgical masks and the cloth masks available to most customers capture some spittle when sneezing, coughing, and talking. they aren't a magical barrier even when used correctly. they don't prevent infection, they just lower transmission rates (effective r0) by minimizing the how far droplets from your sneeze or cough can travel so that the majority (though not all, and not aerosolized virus) is caught within the mask.

i've seen employees in proximity to customers and coworkers on multiple occasions not using their masks to cover mouth and nose. yesterday, a worker wearing a surgical style mask repeatedly walked up within 2 ft of me to ask if she could help me find anything. i said no the first time. on the third time within less than 5 minutes of entering the store, she approached while i was bent down reading eye drop labels on a lower shelf to determine which would treat the allergy symptoms of my teen. i became exasperated and told her that i had already told her twice that i didn't need help. furthermore, i explained, i was trying to socially distance and she kept stepping needlessly close. she said "i'm sorry" and then immediately crouched down next to me almost shoulder to shoulder adjusting items a foot farther down the shelf. she had not been stocking in the aisle when i entered it a moment before. exasperated, i grabbed the eye drops and finished up without buying the two other items i came for, including waiting in line for a prescription that was ready for pick up.

it's not like i looked like a shoplifting risk or something and needed to be tailed the whole time i was in the store. i'm a middle-aged woman in business casual.

background- i used to work in epidemic response at cdc in very restrictive ppe conditions. proper use of ppe is not intuitive or natural , it must be taught and continually reinforced. i blame this store's management for the repeated examples of improper use of ppe or lack of distancing awareness that i've observed on every recent visit. things seem to be even more lax now that customers are all wearing masks- the employees seems to have a growing false sense of security. this puts employees and customers unnecessarily at risk. i'll be looking for a new pharmacy until there is a vaccine or i have confirmed antibody titers from an fda-approved serological test.

i was just traumatized at the memorial er hospital in southbend today.  i had been exposed to the coronavirus but was told my results would not be back for 7-10 days.  meanwhile, i got worse but then i got better, but then two days ago, i had taken a turn for the worse--fever, chills, cough, etc., all those symptoms came back with a vengeance. so, upon hearing that it could take up to 10 days for my results to come back, i looked at my sons and told them i couldn't wait any more. i had to go to the er. we called the cdc to see what we needed to do. they told me to call the er, so they could prepare for me. 

i called the memorial hospital er, and they told me to just go in and register. however, after self-quarantining for 8 days, i was not about to go into a public population and possibly expose anyone if i had the coronavirus. my brother called the hospital  and they gave him different instructions for me to follow, which was call them when i got to the er, and someone would come out to me. 

none of this protocol was followed once i arrived. i was told to just go in. yep. i refused to go in, so my brother called the hospital again, and the lady informed him that if someone is telling me to go in, then i should just go in. (all recorded by the way.)

now, i'm going to move directly to the er room with the doctor, and this is where i was completely traumatized, accused and made to feel like a criminal. (i'm a 56 year old professional--educator). 

the doctor came into the room and goes to listen to my lungs. he twists my shoulders away from him. (i get it, and i'm okay with it.  he didn't  want me to breathe on him), but then he used his elbow to turn my head so it faced the door. then after he had listened to my lungs, he started asking why i came to his hospital to expose people if i had the coronavirus . (i forgot to mention that an iv had been put in my arm but not taped down because the nurse had forgotten the tape, and at this point,  i totally understood that they wanted to spend very little time in my room in case i'm positive--and i'm okay with it up until this point.)

i had mentioned the iv to the doctor when he first came into my room, and i even told him that the iv looked like it had twisted in my vein.  while this doctor was on a tirade, blaming me for being at the hospital and accusing me of spreading sickness to everyone, he reached across the left side of my bed and jerked, not pulled, the iv out of my right arm. he then left while i was bleeding in that room. 

i called my brother, crying and panicked, and my brother told me to take pictures of everything. because of my hysteria, i had only taken two pictures when a nurse came into the room, telling me to calm down. i showed her my bleeding arm and told her that i couldn't calm down informing and showing her what the doctor had done to me. (by the way, my brother was still on the speaker phone.) the nurse then threatened to call security to take my phone if i took another picture. my brother then spoke up and said no one better not touch my phone or they would be sued. 

while i was still upset and crying, my brother called the administration of the hospital and informed him how i was being treated. 30 minutes later, the doctor came back into my room to apologize because he said it had been years since he had done an iv, and he didn't know that when he pulled my iv out like he had done that i would bleed like i did.  he then proceeded to say everyone's nerves were on edge because of the coronavirus. i continued to let him try to explain why i he had treated me so horrible. 

when he finished, i then reminded him that i had complied with everything that i had been told to do while awaiting my test results and that i had come to the hospital because i was getting worse instead of getting better--only to have a doctor accuse, blame and make me feel like criminal--when all i was seeking was medical help.

i still don't know if i'm positive or negative. i'm still waiting for my results to come back, and i've been on self-quarantine for 8 days. my nerves are also on edge, and a medical doctor traumatized me when i needed reassurance.  i'm the one who has done everything i've been told to do--not going out partying, gathering in groups, etc..  

i have self-quarantined for 8 days now, and i needed reassured that i was going to be okay today. attached are the two pictures of how the doctor left my room after jerking the iv out of my arm. today, i needed a doctor who was at his best to take care of me, not a doctor who was stressed whose nerves were on edge. i had gone to this hospital for medical treatment, but instead, i left completely traumatized.

tl;dr - choose another pediatrician, even if you have to wait. 

after recently moving back to the area, i had chosen a pediatrician for my daughters 12m visit. unfortunately, due to the pandemic, they were booked solid for two weeks and i needed to find another pediatrician if i wanted her immunizations on time. i called around to several, and most were not accepting new patients (unless newborn) or had very long waits. when i called dr.o i asked the same two questions i always ask; "are you accepting new patients?" and "do you take our insurance?" yes, and yes. they set the appointment and took her insurance information over the phone. 

the day prior to the appointment, they shut down the location she was set to go, and rescheduled us for another location on the same date. they took our insurance information over the phone once more. the day of the appointment, they called us to see if we wanted to move our appointment time up, and we did not (that's impractical with a baby...) but we did make our scheduled time and we once more gave our insurance information. we filled out the documents in office, and gave the actual card to the receptionist, who told us we owed nothing as it was a well check. 

nine days later, we got a call from them stating we owed the full amount, that they didn't take our insurance. she said the office visit was going to be $200 & the vaccines would be at cost... well imagine my surprise when i got a $1200 bill! they then reduced said bill down to just over $700. 

seven hundred dollars for a well check and vaccines! after taking our insurance three separate times! scam! as for the bill itself, it does not list what any of the charges are for. scam! 

as soon as this pandemic is over, every mommy and me group, every play date, every library story time, every park - i will be making sure everyone knows: do not go to dr.o!

during the coronavirus/covid-19 issue in march 2020 i needed to go in to get my standard bloodwork drawn.  

like a good patient, i made an appointment far in advance so i could come in early since i was fasting for 12 hours and would be hungry.  making an appointment does a number of things: it assures that i will be seen within five minutes of my appointment, regardless of how many "walk-in" persons there are and it also lets quest know how busy it will be so they can ensure enough staff are at hand. 

when i walked in this time, the waiting room was elbow-to-elbow full of people, violating social distancing regulations.  i had my face mask on and i checked in with the computer as i would normally do.  i noticed on the television there were a number of "walk-in patients" already registered -- this isn't a concern to me, as i made an appointment for 08:15 and it was 08:02 when i checked in.  normally, my name would rise to the #1 spot because i was only person who bothered to make an appointment.  this time it was different.

my name stayed on the bottom of the queue at slot #10 with an 'estimated' waiting time of 104 minutes!!!  i took these photos at 08:11 to prove this actually happened. as i am classified as a person vulnerable to catching covid-19, there was no way i could allow myself to remain in a tiny room of people coughing and sneezing.  when the phlebotomist came out, who appeared to be the only person working at the time, i said to them that i had an appointment and was a vulnerable patient and couldn't remain in this environment, she shrugged her shoulders and said "just leave then".

i've been treated badly at quest labs a few times (mainly from their terrible billing people who don't seem to know to credit someone's bill when an hsa pays it), but this was the first time they were that rude!

so, i left.  i filed complaints with all the appropriate health agencies and quest's main office and shall never return to this location -- perhaps never to quest again!

wow. i am seriously confused about the special snowflake-ism that runs rampant in some specialties around here!  you stare into vaginas all day, people, you're not wilhelmina vautrin or alan turing or desmond tutu (or nelson or lincoln or ... and the unendable list goes on (and on) ;p).  and yet, you call for an appointment, you leave very specific information as to what you need (as one does in such medicine), and when valerie, who sounds like she, at best, woke up on the wrong side of the bed, and at worst, thinks you're incredibly stupid and unbearable for some unknown reason gives you a call back to schedule, it's like pulling freaking teeth!  i get a gyne and a dentist all in one!  great!

so, today when valerie calls me, she asks me that question a person just can't bear, right? "what was it that you need?" like... you didn't already say, and like you called them ordering hamburgers instead of needing to see a physician. 

you repeat yourself, because you really need this, and when you tell her that very specific thing you need again, asking if that's something the doctor has history or marked experience in, she says in a tone like you're torturing her loved one, "i really don't know all the things the doctor knows." 

she's not meaning she's never gone to medical school, she's flatly replying that she doesn't have any clue what specified medicine the doctor has in her brain-vault!  okay, fine, that's why you asked before she called you back, but let's be awesome and move on from that point.  except, wait for it... wait for it... "did you read the blurb on the website that tells you about the doctor?" hah. -cough- sorry.  valerie wonders if you hopped online to see if this was something the good doctor could handle, while, valerie, the person behind the desk returning phone calls since 8:00 this morning (she called us at 8:30), working for said doctor doesn't even know.  apparently hasn't read the blurb. if you weren't hacked before, you are now.

so, you tell valerie if she has no interest asking, that's fine, maybe this isn't a good fit, and she now sounds like we've kicked her puppy through a fan as she puts us on hold and drops the call.  well.  did we really expect anything different?  

you find yourself wondering if that's that... you figure, okay, you'll wait a little while, surely this isn't as bad as it _feels_.  they'll just return that call that "their system" "accidentally" "dropped" and you'll get the great answer to what appears to be unknowable...  but by 8:56 no one has called back.  

okay then.  you already know this isn't an appointment you're going to keep or even take, but for kicks and grins (i mean, she did wake you up at 8:30), you call back and are all like, "hi valerie, it's (your name).  you called me a while ago and you were gonna check to see if the doctor could handle that problem we discussed, remember? right as you put me on hold, your system dropped the call.  i waited half an hour and no return." valerie stutters for a few seconds, then finally gets it together enough to say this, "yeah, i saw the phone, we've just been handling other calls this morning."  and there it is. 

l.o.l.

i'm a chill person.  i've got a problem and i'm looking for a reasonable, experienced, decent human of an md to maybe help me fix it.  this problem i have has been an excruciating situation that's been affecting me for almost 30 years (and when i say excruciating think putting out lit cigarettes on sensitive body parts, yeah) and, yet, even with all that, i still manage to be a pretty chill person.  i honestly just wonder... what's their excuse?

if i could put 0 stars, i would. either these guys are not equipped with the info to handle covid-19, or they personally are deceptive enough to get me in and waste my time so they can just accumulate money when i'm vulnerable.

first red flag; the nurse that was out front was wearing gold shoes - like shiny gold shoes, like he was rich or something. i don't think that fits the dress code. was nice and gave me a mask (i can't find masks anywhere), but he didn't seem to give me clear info and directed me more to the front desk so i could talk with them. i talk with the lady, but she's the same way; she urges me more to talk to the doctor and withholds information about what people are really supposed to be doing for covid-19. i was very vulnerable and crying because i've been having very faulty insurance issues and getting testing goes against what i think, but i'm still worried from the contradicting info i've been getting. she clearly didn't want to deal with me and rolled her eyes and was very apathetic. i gave her my info, but the more i talked, the more i felt it would be a good idea to leave because i wasn't showing extreme symptoms. i asked her if i could just go and leave, and she says, "you want to check out?" i say yes, thinking she means to let me be on my merry way somewhere else. she gives me back my info and everything in my gut tells me to run out the door before anything, but i see the bracelet she made, and it was the opposite. i felt trapped. i have a tendency to trust people too much when vulnerable, and didn't know how to say "no" to this because i was sure i needed the testing to get pay for being out of work. i'm freaking out about the charges, but it seemed like she just wanted me to go in so she didn't have to deal with me. i talk with the person checking me in, crying and having another meltdown and she rolls her eyes at me, too, like money is nothing to cry about. i'm sure this person at least knows they don't have the tests. i'm sure she does. after a long ass wait, same thing. every person who deals with me this whole time is apathetic to my feelings including the doctor. they're very dismissive and really don't give a shit.

at the end, i'm still crying and bawling because i literally came in and am going to spend shitloads of money on an er bill that did nothing for me. and they didn't give a shit this whole time.

they could have solved this whole problem, with, "well, most people with your symptoms are staying home, because it's only really troublesome if you have breathing problems and other of the major symptoms," "we don't have the test for minor people because we're in limited supply, so if you feel for sure it's serious, go in," (before the doctor told me), or just be understanding when i explain all the symptoms. the goal with hysterical customers is to be patient, listen, and really try to understand what they're saying and try to help calm them down. these people were doing none of the sort. they always called someone else over just as assholish as they were, if not more. the last guy who walked me out just thought i was some freeloader. and he's like, "why are you crying?" and he's clearly very annoyed and doesn't care and is flippant about my words and feelings. at the end, i realize the reason i'm upset if because i feel the front desk lady tricked me into going in, "and he's like, well, you should talk to her about that, not me." again. no one gave a shit. at all. the whole time. people are human and this covid-19 is making people paranoid for no reason because all the info from media is wrong.

a friend who works with lab test info that doctors send her later text me all the info i needed to know about this after i explained it to her, and she said there were many doctors not prepared to handle this virus at all and aren't following proper etiquette in dealing with it. she explained many doctors in general are not following proper etiquette cdc gave them for covid-19. she said these medical staff were not handling it appropriately. so she confirmed the most important part of the whole thing.

you guys really need to hire more compassionate staff who know how to de-escalate situations, particularly more with staff at the front. also, you guys need to be way more educated about this virus.

i haven't been in a hospital since i was two years old having my tonsils out. seriously, several decades (like 6?). and during this covid-19 pandemic, a hospital is the last place i want to set foot in. but my doctor ordered an echocardiogram for me anyway and off i went to the imaging dept at legacy meridian park medical center. 

upon entering the main lobby, i was directed to sanitize my hands, secure my mask and had my temperature taken (96.8 thank you very much). the imaging technician, eric, came out and directed me to the procedure room. i had to put on one of those ridiculously small hospital gowns and lye on my side on the imaging table. if you've never had an echocardiogram, it's basically a test that uses ultrasound to show how your heart muscle and valves are working. the sound waves make moving pictures of your heart so your doctor can get a good look at its size and shape. it's totally painless, although the clear gel they use to get the instrument to glide over your skin is hella cold! being a big chicken, i kept my eyes shut tight and didn't look at the monitor as eric worked. my test took less than an hour and included an injection of dye to get a really clear picture. a technician from the physiology dept was on-call to insert the iv for the dye. he saw my anxiety and joked by asking me where i'd like him to stick the needle to start the iv. i told him i had no idea, wherever was easiest for him. "how about your neck?" he smiled and i laughed out loud. everything was ok after that.

my whole experience was phenomenal! every staff person i met was professional and empathetic. covid-19 protocols were being strictly followed and i couldn't have asked for better care.

nordon's voice mail system makes it hard to speak to anyone, and suggests instead that emails - which are ignored - be sent. a request for refills emailed on a thursday was not filled until monday, only after an argument with the pharmacist, who claimed that he arrived to 500 emails that morning, and had 61 prescriptions to fill before mine. i wonder why, if the shop is that busy, they've begun to close on sundays, there never seem to be more than three customers in the store, and there's never a line to get inside. on a monday morning in a well-run pharmacy, how could there have been 61 prescriptions ahead of a refill request sent the previous thursday?
